subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE

speechtext: Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 66, to amend the Canada Evidence Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OF BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
The purpose of this
bill is to submit for the consideration of parliament an amendment following a recommendation of the commissioners on uniform legislation of the Canadian Bar Association. It would add a section to the Canada Evidence Act to make admissible as evidence photographic copies of entries in the books of banks or of the dominion government or of any of its departments, and incidentally permit the destruction of voluminous old records, thereby saving considerable storage space. A similar bill has already been adopted by five of the provincial legislatures and is being considered by the others.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

WHEAT ACREAGE REDUCTION BONUS
speechtext:
1.	What are the names and addresses of the persons to whom cheques were issued (a) for over $10,000, (b) for $5,000 to $10,000 on wheat acreage reduction bonus?

subtopic: WHEAT ACREAGE REDUCTION BONUS
speechtext:
This question has been given further consideration and I would still suggest to the house that it be dropped, on the grounds stated a few days ago. I have no objection at all to the names being given to any member of the house who desires to have them, but I hesitate to set a precedent by bringing down a list of names out of a group of 186,000. It would require a great deal of work by the staff, and, if given with respect to this legislation, similar information might be asked for in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and other measures of the kind. It would entail an enormous amount of work if the house were to take the position that all these names must be given, together with the amounts received.
Only seven names are involved in this particular list. Three of them are names of companies, and four I think are names of individuals. I do not know any of the individuals except one in Saskatchewan; the others are in Alberta. There is no personal reason, involving the individuals themselves or the companies or the government, why these figures should not be given, and as I have said, I have no objection to giving them to any individual member who desires to have them. But companies have asked us for lists of these names for the purpose of using them in making collections. I do not want to be misunderstood when I say that. It is not a question of the individual, but they want these lists of names in groups in order that they may send out their collectors to make collections. We have not thought it proper to turn over to them lists which might be used in that way. They could be got indirectly through people asking for certain names in certain areas and by giving certain dates. But we hesitate to have that done, and for that reason I suggest that the question be dropped.

subtopic: WHEAT ACREAGE REDUCTION BONUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is dropped I would point out that a matter of principle is involved. If the government feels that it is not in the public interest to give certain information to the house, the government may withhold that information; or if giving it would entail too great an amount of work, the information may 'be withheld. But in this particular case there are only seven names, and regardless of everything else I think as a matter of principle we 
should insist upon this information being given to the house. I have asked from my place for the amounts paid to certain persons in the lower categories, and no objection was ever made to giving me that information publicly in the house. As to giving such information to companies which ask for lists of names, that is a different matter. But when members of the house ask for details of the expenditure of public moneys, for the information of parliament, I think the principle is sound that we should be given the information, and on that ground I hope the question will not be dropped.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT POSITION-ACTION OP SOUTH AFRICA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT POSITION-ACTION OP SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he can confirm or otherwise the rumour that the Union of South Africa has ceased diplomatic relations with Vichy, and whether he can make any statement on Canada's relations with Vichy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT POSITION-ACTION OP SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I would say to my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition that I believe the statement that South Africa has severed diplomatic relations with France is correct.
The severance of diplomatic relations between countries is always a serious and regrettable matter, and it would be doubly serious and regrettable, I think, in the case of countries which have been as closely associated as have Canada and France for a period of three centuries. Also, at a time of war, a matter of such grave concern should, I feel, be considered not only in the light of the feelings or interests of one's own country but also in the light of how one country's action may possibly affect the interests and relations of other countries with which it is allied. For that reason our government have felt it advisable to have a very complete exchange of views between the government of the United Kingdom and ourselves and the government of the United States and ourselves, before reaching a final decision * with respect to the attitude which Canada should take towards France as a consequence of developments in that country in the last few weeks. This exchange of views is still in progress. I am not in a position to make a statement this afternoon, but I shall be, I expect, in a position to make a statement to the house when hon. members reassemble on Tuesday next.

subtopic: SOUND REPRODUCTION RECORDS FOR USE OF THE BLIND TO BE TRANSMITTED FREE OF POSTAGE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SOUND REPRODUCTION RECORDS FOR USE OF THE BLIND TO BE TRANSMITTED FREE OF POSTAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in Canada books for the use of the blind are transmitted free of postage under section 47 of the Post Office Act. In recent years an entirely new method of publishing books for the blind has been developed and is widely used by blind people throughout the country, namely, sound reproduction records or "talking books." It is understood that there are as many blind readers in this country reading from sound reproduction records as there are from the conventional books in raised type. In view of this fact I have in the interests of the welfare of the sightless people of this country issued instructions to the effect that sound reproduction records for the use of the blind may be considered as books for the use of the blind within the meaning of the Post Office Act and as such will be transmissible in the mails free of postage. This change will become effective immediately on publication of the usual notice in the Canada Gazette, which I expect will be this week.

speechtext:
An order in council
was passed after the house rose last evening, and the passing of that order in council resulted in an announcement being made to the press. The reason for making an announcement last evening, as the hon. member who is asking the question knows, was the fact that to-day is the cheese board day and biddings on cheese will be made to-day all over eastern Canada. If an announcement had not been made last night, if it had been made to-day or to-morrow, considerable loss might have been taken by certain people who are dealing in cheese to-day. The new agreement entered into with the British government is to be effective from April 1 until April 1 next. I have here a summary of the agreement which I think I should place on Hansard.
The arrangement provides for the sale to the United Kingdom ministry of food of 55,800 tons, 2,240 pounds per ton, or approximately 125,000,000 pounds of cheese from the Canadian production of the fiscal year 1942-43. The ministry also agrees, subject to freight being available, to purchase such additional quantities within their requirements, as Canada may have available for export.
A schedule of quantities to be shipped each month from the present time to the end of April, 1943, is provided and the ministry assumes responsibility for providing marine
Cheese Agreement

transportation. Payment will be made by the ministry to the extent of 90 per cent of the value as soon as possible after the cheese are shipped and the remaining 10 per cent of the value will be paid within 28 days after arrival of the cheese in the United Kingdom, or in the event of the steamer being lost, within 28 days of the estimated due date of arrival.
The shipping schedule will necessitate storing of considerable quantities of cheese in Canada to await shipment during the months of scant production. Last year 90 per cent of the value of cheese held in storage by licensed exporters for later shipment was paid by the ministry of food when the cheese were placed in storage. This year the Canadian government will make the initial payment of 90 per cent of the value to the licensed exporters when such exporters place the cheese in storage, for export during subsequent months. When the cheese are shipped the ministry will reimburse the Canadian government for the advanced payment made to the exporter. This change in procedure of payment is designed to simplify accounting for the ministry of food.
Accuracy of weights is to be verified by the official weigher appointed by the Montreal board of trade, under authority of act of parliament. Such verification will be checked from time to time by an officer of the Department of Agriculture. The quality of the cheese is to be determined by graders of the staff of the Dominion Department of Agriculture. The prices to be paid f.o.b. ocean steamer Montreal or f.o.b. car Montreal for export through the winter ports are:
Cents per pound
For first grade (92 score and over)..	20
For second grade (87 to 91 score)...	19-50
For third grade (under 87 score)______	19
The ministry of food has intimated that the prices specified are higher than may be desirable in view of the probable effect that postwar conditions may have on the markets for cheese, but that subject to due consideration by the government of Canada of the proposed price in relation to post-war developments, the ministry of food is prepared to approve the agreement.
By way of explanation of that statement, which is taken out of the order in council, possibly I should say that the British government was concerned about the advisability of their agreeing to a payment of 20 cents per pound at this time. They believed that if they agreed to pay that it might have some effect upon the price which would be required from Canada for cheese after the war is over. They suggested that if the dominion government

would take the responsibility for saying that this price was necessary to production in Canada at the present time and that it would not necessarily affect prices when the war is over, then they were prepared to agree to it for this year. I may say that it was discussion over that point which somewhat delayed the announcement being made. We had hoped it would have been made not later than early in the month of March rather than at this time.
Information available indicates that Canada may supply not more than approximately 15 per cent of the cheese which the United Kingdom will receive during the current year, and in view of increased costs of labour and supplies required in the production of cheese, the prices provided in the agreement are not considered out of line with increased costs of production. The agreement has received formal approval of his excellency in council and, as already stated, the ministry of food has intimated it is prepared formally to approve the agreement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR

speechtext: Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 65, to assist war veterans to settle upon the land.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Before this bill is given second reading and passed on to the committee, there are certain remarks and suggestions I wish to offer. I approach this subject as one who has had close and intimate contact with those who went on the land under the old soldier settlement scheme, known as the soldier settlement board scheme, and I know something of the tragedies as well as some of the successes of that scheme. At the outset I wish to compliment the minister upon the forward step made in this bill. But knowing what has happened in the past I have one or two further suggestions to make.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) the other evening, following the fine speech made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons), suggested to the government that in the allocation of money or the settlement of men under this scheme his particular constituency or the province of Ontario be not overlooked. Might I point out this interesting fact, that when the soldier settlement scheme was put into effect many years ago British Columbia put more soldier settlers on the land than the provinces of Ontario and Quebec combined. In fact almost as many ex-soldiers settled in British Columbia as in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces. Therefore we in British Columbia were more concerned, shall I say, and had' closer contact with the welfare of the men, than perhaps hon. members from some other provinces.
My first suggestion is in regard to amortization. The committee might very well look into the matter of straight annual payments rather than amortization, because if one looks at the scale of moneys payable over the years he will see that, under the amortization plan as proposed, a settler in ten or twelve years would pay less principal and more interest than he would under straight annual payments.
I am very well pleased that the suggestion has been made to reduce the interest from 5J per cent to 3| per cent, but I say frankly to the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that he might just as well face the issue now and consider reducing the interest for those under the present soldier settlement scheme. They are now paying 5 per cent, and the government and members of parliament are going to be faced with this very issue. The veterans of the last war are going to ask: "Are we not as good soldiers as the soldiers of this war? We also offered our lives and services in 1914-18 and so should receive like consideration." I warn the government that they might just as well now look to reducing the interest under the old scheme from 5 to 3| per cent. Up until the end of last year the tot^l amount paid in under the soldier settlement scheme, in principal, was something over $31,000,000, whereas the interest payable totalled $24,670,190. While many reasons have been given why men left their farms under the soldier settlement board, to my way of thinking one of the grievous enactments was the 5 per cent interest rate. In the lean years and years of depression the debts of the soldier settlers mounted up, and many instances could be cited where after ten or fifteen years of toil and payments, soldier settlers found themselves owing more money to the government than they did when they first entered the scheme.
We hear a great deal about a new order after this war. I am going to leave this thought with the ministry and hon. members of this house: if we are thinking of that new order, why should not a start be made now in this bill? I am not unmindful of the far-reaching effect this bill will have, but I suggest that consideration be given to the scheme in operation in Australia. There if a man purchases land under a land settlement scheme-I am speaking of ex-service men particularly-he knows from the day he goes on that land that no matter how good or how bad the times are he will not be required to pay any more than the original debt. In other words the debt to the government is tax free.
I know there are those who were disposed to laugh when the leader of the Social Credit group the other day spoke about making a grant of farms or land to these men. After all, is there anything extraordinary or out of the way in giving to the men who offered their lives a portion of this good land of ours? Looking at the losses the government incurred under the old scheme, I say in all sincerity that we could very well have given the land free to every man who came under the old soldier settlement board scheme at its inception, and we would still have been money ahead, because, as has been pointed out by the minister, some $4,000 per capita has been lost under that scheme. I believe that $4,000 average is somewhat more than the average debt incurred by each settler under the original act.
Veterans' Land Act

I am therefore suggesting that the committee give some consideration to the Australian scheme. After all what is the real intention of this act? Is it to establish men on the land after the war? I know there are doubts in the minds of some hon. members as to why we should place men on the land at all, but in a country such as ours soldier rehabilitation must embrace some land scheme.
One of the important points not touched on by the speakers the other evening was the economic conditions which may exist after this war. While the minister pointed out that $144 per annum would be the total amount any soldier taking up land would have to pay under a total scheme-by which I mean one involving the limit of $3,600 plus $1,200 for stock and equipment-it should be remembered that to this amout must be added taxes and insurance premiums, so that roughly speaking a man taking up land under this scheme will be called upon to pay at least $200 a year. I think I can speak fairly well for the farmers of the province of British Columbia when I say that in many years few farmers can pay a debt of $200 and live decently. If you have no markets and cannot sell your goods, the amount of interest and even the unpaid principal will become a very great hardship indeed. I suggest for the consideration of the committee that the government might very well absorb these interest charges. According to the figures given by the minister when speaking on the resolution, $1,000,000 a year would, I believe, take care of all the interest which would be charged those taking advantage of this scheme. It might be well worth considering whether, when we help these men go on the land, we should further burden them with interest payments.
I am not so much enamoured of the suggestion contained in the resolution that the director should have the right to sell out any settler. We should be very careful in transferring a right of that kind from parliament to an individual. Remember that under this scheme a settler will be required to pay taxes. If he does not pay them he may be sold out by the municipality, subject of course to the interest retained in the land by the director or the board. But I doubt the wisdom of giving the director absolute power to sell out a settler in the event that such settler should fall down in his payments.
Another suggestion I have to offer is that the act should not be put into operation until the end of the war. I fdar that if we start in on, this scheme now, by the time the war ends so many things may be said against it 
that there will be no inducement to the great majority of the men, who might otherwise do so, to go on the land at the conclusion of the war. When this act is passed it should contain a clause providing that it shall not become operative except by proclamation; and I commend that suggestion in all seriousness to the committee that is to study this measure. I am particularly interested, however, in the "no interest" clause; for I believe that if you relieve these men of the payment of interest you will not only remove a great burden from their shoulders but you will give them more hope and more incentive to pay up and establish themselves permanently on the land.
There was one other thought I wanted to leave with the committee. I believe this scheme envisions a man working partly on the land and partly in industry. This idea was suggested many years ago by Henry Ford, who had) a scheme for establishing small Ford factories all over the country in which men might be engaged for five or six months of the year and sustain themselves for the remainder of the time by working on the land. Perhaps that is what is in the mind of the government in connection with this scheme, but it will not work in British Columbia. Later I intend to have a great deal more to say with regard to the centralization of industries in this country, which to my mind at any rate is going to bring about a troublesome uneconomic condition after this war is over. We have practically no industries at all in the Fraser valley, and I might almost say few in British Columbia, and I am just wondering where the men who take up land in that province, especially those who have only small farms, will be able to find employment. In the past in British Columbia many men went on the land with the intention of ranching; many others went in under the old soldier settlement board, and after they got settled on the land they all had to find additional employment somewhere in order to earn einough money to keep going.
Many of those who reside in the cities believe that a man on the land gets all his food free, that his eggs, his milk and everything else come to him without cost. To those who have that mistaken idea I want to say that generally speaking it costs the man living in the country these days more for his goods than it costs the man in the city. If he does get eggs he has to buy wheat and other grain to feed his chickens; if he does get milk he has to buy feed for the cow, so that his food does cost him more than his labour. I make this statement because I

Veterans' Land Act
rather got the impression the other day that some hon. members had the feeling that a man living in the country could manage to exist without any monetary cost at all.
I apologize for having taken up the time of the house to this extent, but having dealt with this matter for a great many years I thought I should offer these suggestions in the hope that they will be given every consideration when the committee meets to study this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Before this bill is given second reading and sent to the appropriate committee I should like to offer a further suggestion which perhaps has not been particularly emphasized heretofore in this debate. I have often wondered why so much was said about the advantages of a new act as compared with an old one. It seems to be becoming almost a byword to say that a certain act is a great improvement over the old act, and so on; but I could never understand why, if that were so, the old act-whether this act or another one- was not changed and improved when it was found to be unworkable.
During the course of the debate on this bill many hon. members have said that of course this act does not in any sense guarantee security for the soldiers who will be settled on the land. Obviously, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) mentioned the other day, governments have no control over the sunshine and the rain. They have no control over the forces of nature, and many things may happen in the intervening years to make the situation desperately hard for these soldiers who will be settled on the land. We cannot help the reverses that nature may bring us, but we can so frame our legislation as to give these men the security they deserve. I do not believe anyone will disagree with the principle that any soldier who offers his life, as he faces shot and shell in bloody battle, on his return should be offered security for the rest of his life. I am not going to enlarge on the details and ramifications as to what he should do and what the governments should do. The principle that any soldier who offers his life in defence of his country upon his return should be given security for life, should be made clear and clean-cut. We do know that that has not been done.
I have a suggestion for the committee which will review the bill and will have power to make amendments and dress it up so that it may be acceptable to the house. I visualize that when the bill is passed and the time arrives for the government to purchase land under the scheme, there may be wholesale foreclosures on the farming public of Canada who are to-day in desperate need and debt. They may be made under the assumption that those who foreclose may then offer their land for sale to the government at a price satisfactory to the vendors.
I am suggesting that the committee give this possibility some consideration. We should cooperate with the provinces in bringing about certain just debt laws.
Let us not be misunderstood in this matter. We have never claimed that debt should not be paid. Our stand is quite the contrary, that the adjustment of the fiscal policy of Canada should be such that debts can and would be paid. Under the present fiscal policy of Canada with regard to agriculture, we are fast reaching the place where the sanctity of debt is regarded as being a little bit greater and more important than the sanctity of the home. That should not be so. I agree of course that if debtors throughout the years have had opportunity to pay off their debts and have failed to do so, they must be dealt with accordingly. In Canada agriculture has done its best to pay its way, but it has not been able to get out of debt.
The other day in this debate the Minister of Finance questioned the hon. member for Acadia as to whether the trouble under the old act had been that the land was purchased at the close of the last war, a time when there was serious inflation. I maintain that the difficulty was not so much that the land was purchased during a period of inflation as that a period of deflation was permitted to follow, which no government of that day had power to control. The minister's statement was an admission, not necessarily by his own government, that the government is powerless to control that which the banking institution of Canada can bring on when they desire.
May I go a step farther. It is all right to cry to high heaven and to raise the bogey man of inflation. But so far as the debtor is concerned inflation helps him, because in a period of high prices he is in a better position. If agriculture in Canada to-day were experiencing an inflation of their own commodity prices they would be in a better position to pay off old debts. I am not advocating that there should be inflation, but I am saying that there should not be inflation at one time and deflation at another, a circumstance which will cause even the measure we are now discussing to fall far below our expectations with respect to it.
Veterans' Land Act

I would ask the committee to consider the advisability of suggesting that the government should in some sense be restricted in the purchase of land. My particular suggestion would be that it should be restricted in respect to the purchase of any land which had heretofore been the subject of foreclosure. That may seem to be an extraordinary suggestion, but all things being equal I claim that in the great majority of cases as to lands with respect to which foreclosures have taken place there would be no guarantee of security for those who might take them at the close of this war. I suggest that the committee give serious consideration to placing in the measure a section which would say to the government, "In all purchases of land you must guard against purchasing those which in bygone days have experienced foreclosure." As I said earlier, there is a possibility that there may be wholesale foreclosures as soon as the act becomes effective. In such circumstances the government should be reluctant to make such purchases. There should be something in the act to prevent the repurchasing of that kind of land. If it could not produce to serve the interests of one man, I doubt whether it could produce to serve those of another. If there is one thing above all others we want after this war is over, surely it must be that full measure of happiness and sweet content which every last man in the fighting forces deserves upon his return home.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the special committee to consider settlement on the land of veterans of the present war.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I should like to make a statement on the question of subsidies that are being paid in the application of the price ceiling policy. I am sorry that the statement is long but the subject is an important one; there has been much discussion in the press about it, and I feel that I should take the earliest opportunity in committee of the whole or in the house to make a statement to parliament. I do so in order to make clear 
the policies and principles being followed in the payment of such subsidies and the reasons why they are necessary.
There have been a number of questions asked about these subsidies and some concern expressed about them, both in this house and outside. There have also been some implied criticisms of what is being done, although no very specific or direct criticisms have yet come to my attention. I would like to tell the house as clearly as possible what is being done and why, so that there will be no misunderstanding and so that any comments and criticisms can be both specific and constructive. It is, I believe, the duty of members to understand this policy, which involves substantial expenditures for an essential purpose.
The payment of subsidies is an integral part of the general policy of price and income stabilization. Everyone is well aware that the government last fall undertook a vigorous programme to control prices and to secure the necessary stabilization of wages and salaries to make that effective price control possible. This control of prices was absolutely essential in order to defend this country against inflation and all the difficulties and dangers that it brings, all the chaos that it creates. It was necessary in order to enable us to devote our full effort to the war, unhindered by those difficulties to which inflation gives rise. We were faced with the prospect of a substantial reduction in the supplies available for consumers at the same time that the incomes of consumers were rising much more rapidly than fiscal and financial measures could offset. Prices were bound to go up, and go up rapidly, unless a limit was placed on them. The general method that was used in placing that limit on them by means of an overall ceiling is familiar to the house and was explained initially by the Prime Minister in a broadcast and subsequently in detail to the house by myself. The reasons why that rather drastic method was chosen have been fully explained, and I believe they have commended themselves to the Canadian people as well as to parliament. It has been understood that in order to control the price level, we have had to control all prices and to secure a stability of wages and salaries by means of various regulations.
In carrying out this policy, the wartime prices and trade board, with the approval of the government, has been very firm in refusing to permit any increases in prices above the ceiling. In a very few cases special circumstances have made it administratively impossible, or nearly impossible, to establish or maintain the ceiling; for example, in the case of fresh fruits and vegetables, and

War Appropriation
imported books. But these have been true exceptions and not any relaxation of the general rule. In addition, of course, the board recognizes and permits a normal seasonal variation in certain prices.
After thorough consideration of all the difficulties and all the conditions involved, and after continual re-examination of our experience up to date, the wartime prices and trade board has remained convinced, and the government has remained convinced, that we must really hold prices firmly if we are to hold them at all. We cannot let prices move up first in this sector, and then in that, in response to special conditions or pressures. We must make the ceiling stick. We are not doing this merely as a matter of principle or as a means of rejecting arguments for adjustments; it is being done for good practical reasons. Each increase in prices that we would permit by means of a flexible ceiling would be bound to lead directly to other movements. Sometimes they would lead directly to increases in the prices of goods made from other goods or into which the prices of other goods enter as a cost. In other cases, increases in prices would have their effect on many other prices through bringing about higher wages and consequently higher costs in many other industries. This sort of process would gather momentum like a snowball rolling down hill. It is, we believe, on the basis of all the information we can find, far more practicable and equitable to make whatever adjustments are necessary to prevent any prices from rising than to permit some of them to rise and then to make the necessary adjustments in others. Secondly, it would be manifestly unfair to permit some industries or some trades to increase their prices and not permit others to do so when they had equally valid reasons. Consequently, if we permitted any increases, we would be forced to consider other cases of the same kind throughout the whole economy. We could not, therefore, deal with a few of the most difficult cases without creating other cases at the same time. Thirdly, we wish to carry through a simple, straightforward policy and method that consumers can understand as well as traders. We want the women of this country, who do its shopping, to know what we are doing and to be able to see to it that the regulations are being observed. If we were always tinkering with prices, letting them go up a little here and a little there, the consumer would not be able to understand what we were doing, or to detect any infraction of the price regulations without great difficulty and study.
Finally, of course, we realize that any increase in prices, arising from the shortage of supplies of a particular commodity or service, would prevent some people from obtaining it because they could not afford it, or would force them to do without other things. It would be part of the process of inflation that we are trying to prevent. It would amount to permitting the supplies to go to the highest bidders, rather than to those who most require them. This we wished to avoid, and we do not wish to compromise with the evil that we are attempting to prevent.
From the beginning of our price stabilization policy it has been foreseen and understood that some unusual methods, such as subsidies, or their equivalent, would be necessary to meet a number of the special problems that would arise in carrying out the price ceiling policy. I mentioned this fact in speaking in this house in November on the price control policy, particularly in relation to imports. The British government has been paying subsidies for some time in order to stabilize the cost of living in Britain-actually 125,000,000 pounds last year. We realized that we would probably not be able to escape the necessity of paying subsidies ourselves if we were to succeed in holding prices steady despite rising costs, particularly of imports.
The necessity for subsidies or their equivalent arises from the fact that the costs of providing goods or services to the Canadian consumer cannot be completely controlled or from the fact that in some cases these costs were actually higher at the time the ceiling was imposed than the level of costs that was then being reflected in the prices charged. We can control and hold down most of the costs which enter into prices of Canadian goods and services, but we cannot control them all. In so far as these costs rise beyond the amount which the industry can absorb with fixed prices, we must either do without those goods, or raise the ceiling on their prices, or else pay subsidies or take some equivalent action to meet the rising costs without increasing prices. We have been firmly resolved not to permit the ceiling on retail prices to be increased in order to meet these increased costs. We are prepared to permit some non-essential supplies to disappear from the Canadian market rather than permit either their prices to be increased above the ceiling or to subsidize what are really non-essentials. However, there are a number of essential commodities the costs of which have risen beyond the amount which the industry can
War Appropriation

absorb at fixed prices, and the supplies of which must be maintained in the Canadian market as far as possible, and in these cases we have undertaken to pay a subsidy or else to make bulk purchases of them for government account and resell them to Canadian dealers or manufacturers at prices that will enable them to be sold to the public at the ceiling price.
By far the most important cases where we cannot control costs and where these have risen substantially since the ceiling period are found in the field of imports. This country always has been dependent on a very large variety of imported goods, and particularly of imported fuel, materials and semi-finished goods to be manufactured in Canada. We must continue to import a great variety of commodities in order to maintain essential civilian supplies, as well as for war purposes. Obviously we cannot control the costs of these imports up to the stage where they reach Canada, and these costs have risen in very many cases. In part the increased costs have been due to higher prices and higher costs of production in the United States and in the United Kingdom, where we obtain these goods. In both those countries costs have been going up during the last year, and in the United States prices have been rising rapidly since the time our ceiling was imposed. Furthermore, we have had to pay shipping and insurance costs, which are increasing daily, for all those commodities which reach this continent from overseas, and in some cases we have had to meet the cost of bringing them by more roundabout routes or more expensive forms of transport than would normally be employed. For example, in the importation of some goods from South America, I understand that the normal method was that they would travel approximately five thousand miles by water and five hundred miles by land, and that now, frequently, those same goods travel three thousand miles by water and two thousand miles by rail.
I would like to call the attention of the house to the fact that since the base period used for price control purposes the war has spread over all the oceans of the world, and has caused enormous changes in shipping and in sources of supply. The Canadian consumer has been protected by the price ceiling against any effects of this spread of the war on his cost of living. Without the price ceiling we should all have suffered higher costs of living because of the fall of Singapore and the German submarine offensive off the Atlantic coast. As it is, our prices are not reflecting these very serious developments, but somewhere the cost must be borne, and in part at

least it is being borne in the subsidies we are having to pay on imports in order to make supplies available to Canadians at ceiling prices. The disasters in the far east and the greatly increased scarcity of shipping have also shut off a number of our usual sources of supply and made us dependent upon more expensive sources. Consequently we have had to pay higher prices to obtain things from near at hand or from secondary sources of supply than the prices we were paying at the time the price ceiling was established, when we could buy in much cheaper markets.
As a consequence of all these factors, we have had to undertake to pay subsidies on imports, or in a few cases, to buy imports by means of government agencies and resell them to Canadian producers or dealers. This import policy was announced at the time the price ceiling went into effect. I shall give some details of this policy in a few moments but I wish to say something first about subsidies on commodities produced at home.
Here, the principal increases in costs which have given rise to the necessity for subsidies are those which originate in the difference in time at which things are produced and at which they are sold. The goods that were being sold during the base period from September 15 to October 11 were produced during an earlier period. Sometimes it was much earlier; sometimes it was only a few weeks previously. During the period between the time the goods were produced and when they were	sold,	costs	had	in many casesalready risen, but retailers and other dealers had not increased their prices to reflect the increased costs of producers and manufacturers. In other words, they were not taking an abnormal profit on their inventory. However, when the dealers and retailers had sold the goods	which	they	had	bought at thelower prices before the base period, they had to replace	them	with	goods purchased athigher prices, and yet	they	could not sell
these goods at more than the ceiling price, which was the price they had been selling at during the base period. This naturally reduced the margin between their buying and selling prices, which is the source of their revenue from which they meet their expenses and derive their incomes. It was this rise of costs in relation to selling prices which produced what has come to be called the "squeeze"-I am going to use some phrases now which have formed a limited new vocabulary-and which has caused many of the most difficult problems that the wartime prices and trade board has had to face.

for war production, which, of course, the government would purchase ultimately. Nor are they paid on goods imported directly by consumers themselves, or on goods imported prior to December 1, 1941, or where the increase in cost is trifling, or on goods the production of which is prohibited in Canada, or, finally, on any goods to which the price ceiling does not apply. Most important of all perhaps, from our point of view, a long list of various classes of goods regarded as non-essential was given on which subsidies would not be. paid. Of course, in addition to the restrictions on goods eligible for subsidy, there were also the restrictions under the War Exchange Conservation Act, intended to prevent the use of foreign exchange for the purchase of a great many non-essential goods. Consequently it should be noted that there is a double sieve, so to speak, to prevent the subsidizing of non-essential imports.
It will be noted that in the case of these imports we specified not those goods on which subsidies will be paid, but rather those classes of goods on which subsidies will not be paid. The reason for this is a very practical one. It is impossible to make a satisfactory list of the many thousands of materials and parts and other items that it may be necessary to import into Canada even for ultimate consumers' use. It is more practical to rule out all those classes of goods which we can identify as being nonessential. We have attempted to do that, first under the War Exchange Conservation Act, and again now in excluding them from subsidy. This selection of non-essential goods has been based upon a careful study of our import trade and our tariff items. Quite possibly it is not complete, and it is probable that as we go along we shall be increasingly stringent in classifying goods as non-essential and excluding them from subsidy.
However strictly we draw the line of essentiality, there are bound to be some borderline cases-some items which will appear to some of us as essential and which will appear to others as non-essential. Some types of food, for example, will seem to many of us unnecessary at least in view of what we can substitute for them from our own supplies, while other persons in this country will regard them as valuable articles of diet which cannot be satisfactorily replaced. To decide whether such items should be included or excluded involves questions of judgment which we must decide as best we can and in the light of a developing supply situation. In making any decision of this kind we must take account

not only of the character of the goods themselves and the possibility of substituting others for them, but also the possibility that by excluding them we may divert demand to other items, particularly domestic items, and thereby create serious shortages. We should remember that in those cases where prices have risen substantially when we classify an import item as ineligible for subsidy we are, in effect, placing an embargo upon its entry, and we must be prepared to deny ourselves entirely those supplies. Perhaps I should add that in the case of minor items, it may be possible that traders will continue to import them, even at a loss, simply to maintain certain connections and to continue to supply the markets which have been supplied in the past, but we cannot expect this to happen in any important cases.
In a number of cases it has been possible to avoid or substantially to reduce import subsidies by means of simpler action taken with regard to customs duties and other charges. For example, we hava eliminated dumping duties at this time, since there is almost no danger of unfavourable effects of such action. It has also been provided that on the recommendation of the board in specific cases, invoice values may be accepted for customs purposes instead of home market values, as are normally required. In other specific cases duties have been reduced or eliminated in order to enable goods to be imported at a cost that will make it possible to sell them at the ceiling price.
On other than imported goods, only a small number of subsidies are being paid, and most of them are not yet of significant proportions. Much the most important of these domestic subsidies up to date has been that on milk. This is a temporary subsidy being paid at the rate of 40 cents per 100 pounds for milk used in the manufacture of concentrated milk products, and of 30 cents per 100 pounds on milk sold for fluid milk in all areas where no increase in milk prices took place between August 1, 1941, and the date of the price ceiling.

Well, it does. I have said that this subsidy is a temporary one; already it has been announced that it will be discontinued at the end of this month and a better arrangement of prices for milk products substituted for it, which will enable us to meet our domestic requirements for milk and its products and also the abnormal demand for exports of cheese and concentrated milk products to the United Kingdom. The details of this new scheme were made public this morning.
Another domestic subsidy worth noting is that on the 1941 pack of domestic canned fruits and vegetables. The need for this subsidy arose from the fact that many retailers established their prices in the base period on the cost of these canned goods in the spring and summer of 1941, while the canners, on the other hand, had increased their prices over these levels before the end of the base period, thereby establishing their selling prices f.o.b. cannery quite substantially above those which the retailers had paid. Consequently the retailers were unable to replace canned goods for sale at the retail ceiling prices. In order to enable them to sell at the retail ceiling, it was decided to reduce the cannery prices of these goods, and some of the wholesale prices corresponding to them, to the levels of the spring and early summer of 1941. The costs of these goods have already been incurred and cannot therefore be reduced. It has been necessary, as a consequence, to provide a subsidy to enable these goods to be sold at the lower prices necessary if they are to be moved through the retail channels. Canners are being compensated by 80 per cent of the amount of the reduction in the selling prices that they have absorbed on their inventories, while the wholesalers whose prices are reduced are being compensated to the extent that the f.o.b. cannery price is
44561-1191	*
reduced, but wholesalers are being required to bear the extra carrying charges and sales tax incurred on the higher prices and for which they cannot recoup themselves in their new wholesale prices. Members interested in the details of these operations can find them in a press release and a statement issued by the board on March 24.
Some subsidies are also being paid to permit the sale of leather footwear and of leather clothing at the retail ceiling prices. In the; case of footwear, the problem arose from the fact that the goods sold during the base-period were made back in the spring of 1941 and the cost of manufacturing such footwear increased by some 15 per cent between that time and the base period. Somehow this increase in costs had to be borne without any increase in the retail price, if the principle of maintaining the ceiling was to be observed, as the board felt it must be. After a thorough investigation of all the circumstances, it was decided that part of the increased costs, amounting to about 8 per cent, would be shared equally by the manufacturer, on the one hand, and the wholesalers and retailers, on the other, and that the government, through the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, would pay a subsidy to manufacturers-equal to 7 per cent of the selling price of their shoes to enable them to sell at reduced prices. This subsidy was only to be paid pending the working out of measures to eliminate unnecessary costs. Advisory committees' have been established by the industry to devise methods of simplication and cost reduction, mainly I think by the reduction of the numbers of styles of shoes. Extensive plans are being made to that end. It is the intention of the board to see that as soon as possible costs are reduced to the point where the subsidy can be discontinued.
The case of leather for clothing is more complicated in detail, and I would refer hon. members to a statement of the board, dated February 13, and various orders issued at that time. Again the problem arose from the substantial increase in the cost of production that took place between the time when the goods sold in the base period were manufactured and the time that they were sold, establishing the ceiling for the seller. It was arranged that tanners would reduce their prices of leather below those they received in the base period, thereby absorbing part of the squeeze, some of which, however, was to be borne by the wholesalers and retailers. A subsidy was provided for the tanners to enable them to sell at these specially reduced prices, the amount of the subsidy being related to the reduction in the particular prices concerned. The
War Appropriation

various branches of the industry involved .are being asked to cut their costs as rapidly as they can, in order to make possible the reduction or elimination of the subsidy.
Announcement has recently been made of subsidies to be made available for about 40 grocery items specified in order 116 of the board, dated March 23. The need for this subsidy arises out of the same sort of time lags that have been noted above, in connection with leather items and the 1941 canned food pack. The manufacturers' prices for these goods have increased in the months preceding the base period, and many retailers were selling at prices below those appropriate to the higher manufacturers' and wholesalers' prices prevailing in the base period, although some other retailers had increased their prices to correspond with this rise in wholesale prices. The board and the administrators struggled with the problem created by this situation for months, endeavouring to find the most satisfactory solution to it, meantime imposing a very difficult burden upon many retailers. Finally the decision was reached that the only practicable method to solve the problem was to require the manufacturers to reduce their prices back to June 1941 levels, at which all or nearly all retailers can replace their goods at prices which enable them to sell at their ceiling prices. Those retailers whose base period prices were based upon higher wholesale or manufacturers' prices than the new ones are required to reduce their retail prices by an amount corresponding to the reduction in manufacturers' prices. To enable manufacturers to sell at their lower June prices rather than at the later prices of the base period, despite the increase in costs which occurred in the interval, the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation is preparing to pay them a subsidy based upon and not exceeding the reduction in prices below those prevailing in the base period.
In the case of these grocery items, where the number of producers and dealers will likely prove to be very large and where there will be a difficult problem in assessing how far the industries and1 trades concerned are in fact able to bear the increases in cost without help by way of subsidy, a special condition has been attached to the payment of subsidies to provide a sort of automatic check that will ensure that subsidies are not paid to businesses which do not in fact require them in order to sell at the designated prices. This provision is to the effect that the subsidy shall not increase the net profits of the business after taxes beyond the level of net profits after taxes in the standard period as established for excess profits tax purposes. In order to carry out this
{Mr. Ilsley.]
provision, the corporation will only pay such subsidies in the form of accountable advances and final settlement of the subsidy claim will be delayed until the claimant is able to furnish the necessary information respecting his profits in the fiscal period concerned.

This concludes what I have to say at this time on subsidies or types of subsidies, but there are a few important points about them which I would like to emphasize.
In the first place it should be realized clearly that the subsidies are being paid in the interests of the consumer. They are paid when there is no other way of ensuring adequate supplies of a particular product for the consumer at prices permitted by the price ceiling. In principle, these subsidies are paid to the consumer to keep down the cost of living. In practice, because consumers are so numerous, they are paid to producers or dealers on condition that they maintain supplies and carry out the policy of the price ceiling by supplying goods to others at such prices as will permit them in turn to operate within the limits of the price ceiling.
Any statements therefore that the XY company or the AB company is receiving such and such subsidies are misleading. A subsidy may be of no advantage to the firm receiving it except that it will permit others to continue to buy from it. By law consumers are prevented from buying at higher than ceiling prices. It is an obligation of the government

War Appropriation
1879'
therefore to see -that goods are available at the ceiling prices.
When it has been determined that a subsidy is necessary, the point in the trade at which it is paid is a matter of administrative convenience. Since there are many more consumers than dealers and many more dealers than producers, subsidies (aside from import subsidies) are more likely to be paid to producers. What are in effect subsidies to consumers are paid at a point in the trade where the basis of the subsidies can be most readily and quickly verified.
The second point arises out of the first, and it is that the subsidy paid to any particular industry or any particular firm does not constitute a benefit given to it, for the subsidy is conditioned upon certain action which increases the costs or reduces the receipts of the industry or firm. It is a fundamental principle that the industry or trade receiving a subsidy should bear a part of the increased costs in respect of which the subsidy is paid. In other words, the subsidy, in conjunction with the special conditions attached to it, should leave the industry in a worse, not a better, profit position than before the price ceiling was imposed. The Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation makes every practical effort to check the facts supporting claims for subsidy and the good faith of the applicants, so as to ensure that all payments are within the principles which apply to the subsidy in question. Under the heavy pressure of a programme of such magnitude as universal price control, however, it is necessary to take shortcut methods of investigation, and to apply sound business judgment rather than the exhaustive statistical analysis which a more leisurely examination would make possible. It is essential that claims be dealt with promptly so as to ensure an orderly and continued supply of goods.
The third point I would emphasize is that the board and the government are laying great stress upon the reduction of costs by means of standardization, simplification and the elimination of all unnecessary frills and services. We hope by means of such reduction in costs to eliminate or at least drastically reduce the need for domestic subsidies. I think all business men are anxious to cooperate to this end, because they see the need for it and most of them, we find, are reluctant to accept subsidies from the government, even under present conditions, and they are trying to cut costs so that they will not need to depend on help from us. But the importance of this simplification programme extends far beyond the elimination of subsidies. The reductions in costs that can be achieved by eliminating frills, unnecessary services, unnecessary varieties and patterns, etc.,
are very real national gains at a time such as this. We cannot afford to waste either materials or manpower on frills or fancy varieties. Consequently I am, on behalf of the government, urging the board to press ahead with its cost reduction programme, and I am glad to say that the board itself is equally convinced of the very real value of this part of its work. I certainly hope that all businesses in this country-whether manufacturers or distributors-will cooperate to the full extent of their ability in this simplification programme.
I understand that in some conferences which have been held the question has been raised as to whether this is merely a board programme or whether it is a government programme. I want to make it very clear here to-day that this programme of standardization and simplification and economies in production has the sanction of the government, is in accord with the wishes of the government, and is regarded as extremely important by the government.
In combination with this programme of simplified practice being worked out in cooperation with industry, the system of subsidies constitutes a fully mobile, not static, defence against the pressure of costs on prices. We cannot hold up supplies while we are searching out the possibilities of cost reduction. Subsidies ensure current supplies. Simplification and standardization will reduce costs and permit subsidies to be discontinued. I do not suggest that all domestic subsidies can be thus eliminated, but many of them can and will. I referred earlier to subsidies made available on some 40 grocery items on March 23. Arrangements are being worked out which will eliminate a number of those items from subsidy. The picture which some people have drawn of a system of subsidies to vested interest, a system into which the government would sink deeper and deeper and never be able to withdraw, has no relation to the facts.
I should like to be able to give the house a reasonably accurate estimate of the cost of these subsidies this year and in future, but that is not possible. Their amount will depend on a large variety of circumstances which cannot be foreseen, particularly on the costs of import and of shipping, and on the speed with which savings can be effected by the simplification programme I have just referred to. Subsidies paid on a product of universal consumption will necessarily appear large in total. Of course the saving they make possible to consumers will be correspondingly large. After nearly 5 months of operation of the price ceiling, the subsidies actually paid make quite a small total, about 82,125,000 up to April 21. They will increase,

Yes. In the United States I understand it is thought that unless the price situation is taken in hand, costs may rise at the rate of two or three per cent a [Mr. Ilsley.)
month. If costs were allowed to go; if we were to remove our control and let the price level rise in this country, and it rose not two or three per cent a month but twenty per cent in a year, and it that full twenty per cent were reflected in increases in government expenditures alone, the increased government expenditure would be $700,000,000, because in the next fiscal year our expenditures will be about $3,500,000,000. But the increased cost to the government is not the serious feature of the situation at all; it is not a one-hundredth part of the trouble the country would be in. It is not the taxpayer, as such, that is the victim of inflation, even if he does have to pay $700,000,000 more in the course of a year. It is the workman, the consumer, and practically everybody in the country. And more serious than that, in a period of rising prices such as that everyone begins to try to rectify his own personal situation.	He begins to wonder whether
others are not getting a little better treatment in the situation than he is. The economic situation is changing very rapidly. The person in receipt of a pension says, "I cannot stand this; I have to have an increase in my pension." The wage earner says, "I must have an increase in my wages." Strikes and disputes between labour and capital take place. There are differences of opinion as to the quantum of increase suited to the rising price level, and so on. The result is turmoil and disorder throughout practically all centres of your economy.
As I said last fall, I cannot imagine anything internally which would have a more destructive or disruptive effect on the war effort than a rapidly rising price level in Canada. So that if the cost of these subsidies can be kept within reasonable dimensions-and I am sure it can-it is an insignificant cost to pay, as compared with the evils which we will avoid by using it.

Yes, it is a very reasonable insurance premium.
Attempts to estimate the ultimate annual total of subsidies are likely to be unprofitable because, as I have said, the deciding circumstances cannot be forecast. There are certain considerations worth bearing in mind, however. The fact that a subsidy is paid initially is no evidence that it will be continued indefinitely. Many interim subsidies have been established so that supplies can be obtained quickly and freely. Investigations are now proceeding to determine more precisely the extent to which economies

War Appropriation
and standardization can be effected, and what amount of subsidy, if any, will continue to be required, and whether alternative suptplies are available without subsidy. The basis of subsidies is continually under review. Experience will show which are essential and which are not.
If certain essential supplies are to be obtained, some increases in cost must be paid because those costs cannot be avoided. The question to be decided is whether they will be paid directly by the consumer in the form of higher prices, or by the consumers as citizens and taxpayers through the government treasury. I am satisfied that the cost to the country at large is much less and is much more equitably distributed by meeting these costs at this time by means of these subsidies paid on a conservative basis, rather than through permitting increases in prices above the legal ceiling and leading to great difficulties in the maintenance of the established level of prices.
There have been a number of questions raised concerning the amounts of subsidies paid to individual firms or businesses and requests that such information be furnished to parliament. After very careful study of this subject, I have come to the conclusion that it is definitely not in the public interest currently to give the names of persons to whom subsidies are being paid, or the amount paid to each. To do so would reveal to competitors and others intimate details of the nature and volume of such person's business. The principle of refusing such detailed information has always been followed in connection with both the payment and drawback or refund of duties and excise and other commodity taxes, income taxes and similar items. As I have already emphasized, subsidy payments by the commodity prices stabilization corporation are not really subsidies to any manufacturer, importer or dealer, but are in reality subsidies for the benefit of Canadian consumers, and are paid solely for the purpose of making goods available to consumers at prices prescribed by the board. Consequently the important facts are the amounts of subsidies necessary to stabilize prices of each class or kind of commodities or particular commodities, and not the channels through which such subsidy payments may happen to be made.
Moreover, the conditions attached to the payment of specific subsidies may reflect many different forms of adjustments, and payments to individual businesses could be most misleading without full reports in regard to all the arrangements made with the interested parties. For example, in some cases a subsidy nominally paid to manufacturers or distributors may carry a condition requiring the effect of it to be carried through a line of
dealers until eventually it appears in the cost at the retail store. Another example is the kind of subsidy arranged for milk, in which case it is paid as a matter of convenience to the milk distributors, on the specific condition that it be used to increase the price paid for raw milk delivered by the dairy farmer.
I am confident that when members reflect upon what I have said and the various examples I have given them of these subsidies, detailed information on which is available in the published statements and orders of the board, they will not continue to request information on subsidies currently being paid to individual businesses, which would only be apt to lead to misunderstanding and unfounded charges.
At the same time my feeling is that at the appropriate time information as to the individual recipients of subsidy payments should be given to the members of the house. I have carefully considered methods by which this can properly be done.
First, I was of opinion that I should offer to lay this information confidentially before the war expenditures committee. This course, however, has certain disadvantages. I am afraid that the information would be referred to in the house, not in breach of confidence, but in such a way as to cloak subsidy payments with an air of mystery. This is undesirable and would lead to misconstruction by the public.
The second method that I have considered is to see that the information is presented either in the form of a special report by the board or in the report of the auditor general or the public accounts with the other accounts of the fiscal year. The information would not then be presented piecemeal and with inadequate explanation but would be presented in such a way that the qualifications and conditions necessary to the presentation of a fair and complete picture would not be absent.
It must be remembered that we are in the early stages of a most difficult programme and it is possible that the implications of any method of presenting this information are not fully realized. My present view is that after the end of each fiscal year there should be a complete report of some kind along the lines I have indicated, and that course will be adopted unless, in the meantime, some compelling reason appears why it should not, in which case I will make a statement to the house before the end of the present session, a statement that the house will have full opportunity of debating.
I have given this matter full consideration, and, while I do not ask the committee at this time to accept this disposition of the matter, I wish they would consider it, because I think they will realize this is the best way to handle the situation.

Yes; that particular subsidy has been receiving consideration, and is at the present time.
Before concluding, I would like to say a few words about some of the criticisms that have been made of our subsidy policy. Most of these criticisms have, I believe, been vague and general in nature and of a negative character, rather than constructive. I would urge those who wish to criticize the government's policies both in regard to subsidies and in regard to the price ceiling in general, to be as specific and precise as they can, and. to consider carefully the various alternatives to the policies which they criticize or condemn. It is only when there is an alternative open that criticism is really useful, particularly at a time like this when we must act and act quickly.
There are two general types of criticism to be considered-criticism of .principle and criticism of detail. In regard to principle, I believe I have set forth my views at sufficient length to make clear the answers to many of the points that have been raised. Many of the other criticisms of principle apply really to the whole price ceiling policy, and it would lead me too far afield to go into that at length to-day. However, there are a number of points in regard to subsidies which perhaps it would be well to take up at this time. The first is the charge that subsidies cost a great deal and that we cannot, or should not, afford them at this time. To this I would reply that the real issue is whether the goods in question should or should not be produced or imported under present circumstances. If these goods are required, someone must meet the element of cost being covered by subsidies until the time when those costs can be reduced, if they can be reduced. We feel that the best and fairest method of meeting these additional costs is by means of subsidies paid at the cost of the public treasury rather than through allowing prices to go up, bearing in mind both [Mr. IlsIey.J
the direct and the indirect effects of permitting prices to increase above the ceiling level. Certainly it is desirable, as I have emphasized, to eliminate costs rather than to meet them by subsidy or otherwise, at this time, and it is that which we are attempting to do to the limit of our ability, but until we can achieve those reductions, the subsidies are a useful and sensible means of ensuring supplies in the interim without disrupting our price policy. The cost of them is insignificant in relation to the very real benefits the country is deriving from the successful methods of preventing inflation at this time.
The seconds point I would mention is the suggestion that because we cannot estimate these costs we should not embark on this policy. I do not think a very extended reply is necessary to this point. Obviously at a time like this we must undertake action and measures the cost of which cannot be precisely forecast. If as time goes on we find the cost does become greater than is reasonable, greater than the value of the benefits which we obtain from our price control policy, then we will have to amend our policies, but as yet I see no indication that that contingency will arise.
Thirdly, there is the suggestion that the subsidies benefit or enrich certain producers or dealers. I think that what I have said above demonstrates clearly that these subsidies benefit consumers, and not the producer or dealer except to the extent that they enable the production or importation of necessary goods to be maintained. Subsidies are paid only when they are coupled with measures of control which throw a burden upon those who receive them and the net effect of price control and subsidies inevitably is to worsen and not improve the position of the recipients.
There is a fourth criticism that is suggested in some quarters: that somehow or other these subsidies are inflationary. The argument advanced in support of this point is apparently a subtle or even obscure one, but I think it desirable that we should take note of it. In my opinion, subsidies cannot properly be construed as inflationary. It may be suggested that the government by holding prices down with the aid of subsidies is encouraging the public to buy, and that somehow that is inflationary, and that it would be less inflationary if prices were allowed to rise and thereby cut down the buying of the public. This is certainly using the term "inflation" in an unusual sense. If supplies are dangerously short, their sale should be restricted by other means at this stage, rather than simply by an increase in prices that their producers and sellers are

War Appropriation
allowed to receive. To check sales by permitting prices to rise means in effect rationing supplies to the highest bidders, which means that those who have the long purses will get the most. It does not mean that there will be any fewer goods produced; it means that the people with the big incomes will get the goods. The government decided that that sort of thing should be prevented, and it had the support of the Canadian people in that decision. I believe that now more than ever it has their support. Moreover. if prices of goods were allowed to rise wherever the supply is short, that would put more funds in the hands of those who produce them and sell them, and would enable them to bid up the prices for labour and material to produce such goods, which would certainly be inflationary and might well interfere with our war programme. When we subsidize these items we are able to scrutinize and regulate the amount of production and to prevent this undesirable competition with the war programme and inflationary results. Perhaps those who suggest that the subsidies are inflationary have in mind that they somehow put more funds at the disposal of the producers, who will go on to spend them. This same effect, however, would be produced by a rise in prices, since the producers would obtain additional funds in that process just as they would through the payment of subsidies, and they would not be subject to the same control.
There have not been enough criticisms of detail for me to take them up at any length to-day. Such criticisms are appropriate subjects of discussion in this house, and I would certainly welcome any comments that members can make on the details as I have set them forth and as they are published by the board from time to time. One obvious line of detailed criticism will be as to whether or not various items being subsidized are essential; whether, for example, certain types of imports should be subsidized. That is a live issue at the moment. There are a number of items which we are importing from the United Kingdom and for which we pay in sterling. Under present circumstances it costs the nation nothing, or practically nothing, to obtain these goods as long as the British are able to send them to us, and a small subsidy paid to enable them to come in does serve a useful purpose. Other cases, however, will be less obvious, and undoubtedly members will wish to discuss them. It should be borne in mind that, where prices have gone up abroad or where higher shipping or other costs have increased the cost to us of imports by substantial amounts, to rule such imports ineligible for subsidy means placing an embargo upon their entry into Canada, and means
requiring the public to do without them. We can certainly ask the public to do without many things these days and I think we can take a fairly stern attitude in this respect and secure the wholehearted approval of the Canadian people in doing so. We must also bear in mind at the same time the effects on our own supply condition of diverting demand from imports or from relatively less essential to more essential goods.
Just a word or two in conclusion. I know the committee realizes, as does the public, the magnitude and difficulties of the task that the government has assumed in launching and applying its price ceiling policy. There is general recognition that no more courageous policy and no more difficult administrative task have ever been'undertaken in this or any other democratic country. The work of the wartime prices and trade board and of its chairman has been of an exceptionally high character. Mistakes have probably been made, but these have been minor. On the whole, the price ceiling policy and the work of the board have received the commendation and commanded the admiration not only of the Canadian people but of observers in other countries.
This policy is a test of the capacity of this democracy to organize and discipline itself in such a way as to wage total war on the economic front. I had many misgivings at the outset as to whether we could succeed. I now believe that we can and will. We can only do so, however, if this parliament approaches its task of criticism in the proper spirit. If any hon. member wishes to launch a frontal attack on the ceiling policy, it is needless to say that he has the right to do so. The issue can be squarely joined with such hon. member and the matter fought out on its merits. What I do ask is that if there are any hon. members who feel that way about the ceiling policy, they say so frankly and attack frontally.
If their criticisms are merely criticisms of detail, I ask that they make them -with a due sense of responsibility as to the gravity of the issues involved. Suggestions as to methods in which the policy can be improved in execution are, of course, welcome. These suggestions should, however, be constructive rather than purely destructive. They should take into account not one factor alone in the situation but, as far as possible, all factors in the situation. They should go beyond mere sniping at the board or at the details of administration.
I would like to feel that all hon. members of the house, whether they criticise or praise, will do so in a responsible and patriotic attempt to assist the government in making a success of its efforts to attain an end admitted by all to be of the utmost importance for the welfare of the nation and success in the war.
