If it be in order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few general observations at this stage.
The general statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) is appreciated not only by the house but, I am sure, by the country. But of what the minister said in the last five or ten minutes of his remarks the member for Danforth was not overly appreciative, because I am of opinion that very few members in this honourable chamber would desire to make indirect attacks which might undermine, although the minister did not use that word, the work of the board, rather than make a frontal attack. The minister did refer to indirect criticism which might tend to destroy the structure which he is at present building. With all respect to the minister I do not accept his last remarks, which had a sort of schoolteacher effect upon the mind of the member for Danforth at least.
The minister went to some length to explain that the government had adopted this price ceiling policy and now could not vary very much from it because, if they varied from the principles laid down-I presume when he said "principles" he had also in mind the basic period to which the price ceiling policy applied-not only those charged with the responsibility of producing products for the people of Canada but those who consume the goods, and particularly the housewives who in the final analysis do the greater part of the family purchasing, would be confused.
Just why the forty commodities mentioned in the grocery trade were taken out of the September-October bracket and put back to the June date is something which I hope will be enlarged on while this subject is under discussion. It certainly was confusing to most of those in the trade; and if a subsidy of the amount mentioned by the minister, namely $50,000,000, might obtain in the course of the twelve months, surely there was ample to take care of the period from June to September without confusing the entire section of the trade which had to do with that certain set of commodities. While the subsidy is available to those who are producing goods in the particular class even from June, 1941, the minister will agree with me that raw materials so far as cost of production is concerned, in comparison with other essential goods apart from those that are listed, went through a period of advanced costs from June to September.	The raw
material of the commodities was costing progressively more in June, July, August and September, and then the advance was halted in October. That is quite all right. But to take up that period from June to September

not only will create a hardship, which to some degree will be offset by the subsidies to be paid, but will cause those engaged in the production of these commodities to appear to be asking something which is not in line with what obtained in September and October, and it is going to bear very heavily on the subsidy fund.
The subsidy is to be paid to those who have just cause for compensation in that the ceiling price which obtained in June was much lower than that which obtained in September and therefore they experience a considerable loss in bringing the price back to the June selling price. But it is going to be controlled or checked. I am quite in accord with some method of control or checking. When I interrupted the minister, I did not wish to interfere with the sequence of his remarks, but as they were being read I recognized that he could return to the sentence at the point where he left off and not lose the continuity of his remarks. Under wartime price order No. 116 the base period of four years would govern the maximum profits which could be made by anyone claiming the subsidy. But I think the minister will agree that if during that base period an organization had a loss in each and every year, his putting in that phrase "four-year period" had not to do with the standard profits. I think his sentence should have stopped with the "standard profits in accordance with the act", rather than adding the phrase "over a four-year period".
I was going to ask the minister, although I might defer it to some later stage, whether, before a change is ordered, any contact is made with the trade that are supplying different commodities. There is some criticism that these orders are coming too thick and fast. I would prefer to see these subsidies used more to iron out difficulties to having regulations coming out one after the other, some of which in due course must be rescinded or amended. In other words, I am of opinion that in Canada we who are engaged in industry are getting regulations faster than we can take them,-leaving the impression that our democratic organization known as government has a tendency to become a little autocratic.
There is another observation I should like to make with regard to this ceiling, particularly referring to the June-September reversal or squeeze which caused some squeals and squeaks when it went into effect on March 24 last. The labour costs went on until September, and the cost of living bonus is taking care of the situation fairly well so far as labour is concerned. In passing, may

War Appropriation
I remark that the cost of living index as determined by our bureau does not take care of the actual increase; there seems to be something which is not included. But labour costs rose in that period, and for those manufacturing the goods to have to extract back from this fund the labour costs is just adding another burden. Whereas the industry and the individual workman received their increase, costs in respect of these forty items reversed as at June, although the average cost of living went up between June and September.
In the main this legislation is necessary now. Mark you, I am careful not to say that it is sound for an ordinary economy; it may be sound for a wartime economy. But in the final analysis it is driving individual enterprise to lean on governments and not exercise the initiative which ordinarily we find among the people of our country.
One other observation I should like to make. If the subsidy is going to be paid to any industry, and the sum payable is to be lessened by the amount of excess profits made during the fiscal period under review, then if there are sufficient excess profits in the industry there will be no subsidy, the only subsidy payable being that portion which is left after excess profits are deducted. Then they will find that they come into this difficult field: an industry may be in a score of lines which are not necessarily departmentalized. I think the act covers excess profits made in all lines of business conducted by the particular enterprise making a claim for subsidy.
I warn the minister and the department that this part of order No. 116 of the wartime prices and trade board is going to tend to break corporations down into smaller units. The units which are profitable will probably make their returns under one company, and those that require subsidies for the portion of their business which they are operating at a loss and which comes under this act, will be segregated in a corporation under their control. In that way the provisions of the order of the board providing for over-all profits on all their operations will be circumvented. I mention this as a constructive point, but I am sure that the department is apprised of it. I want it to go out to industry in this country that this parliament is fully aware of what is going on and of what might be running through their minds. I want it to be known that we do not intend to tolerate any circumvention of the act by that particular method.
I hesitate to mention any particular commodity, but this is necessary in order to illustrate the point I want to make, not only with 44561-1201
regard to imports coming into the country, but with regard to exports going out. Because of prevailing prices, particularly in the United' States, the export of certain lines of commodities from Canada has been quite profitable to-some of our United States friends who are in a similar line of trade. Large tonnages of commodities find their way to the United States market, and the result is that there are shortages of raw materials in this country. In order to meet the requirements of Canada, and in view of the fact that there is a ceiling on the selling prices of the finished Canadian products, Canadian industry has had to go farther afield for raw materials. This has caused increased costs, and they have suffered to some extent.
While it is not the example I have in mind, perhaps the one I intend to give will bring this matter more forcibly to the attention of hon. members than anything else. I refer to the export of live cattle, which is causing a shortage of beef . This one industry seems to-be curtailing their production of beef because they were losing a few shekels in that particular branch of their business. I suggest that the government could very well consider this situation and see to it that they keep' on producing the normal requirements of the Canadian consuming public until such time as prices in the United States and Canadian markets adjust themselves. They should not embarrass our Canadian economy by allowing a supply of that commodity to be exported off the market. If subsidies are to be available to take care of excess import prices, some consideration should be given to subsidies to balance export prices.
I am satisfied that in the main industry will work closely with the government to help out during this war-time crisis. I am also strongly of opinion that orders from the wartime prices and trade board1 should be slowed down a little in order to give the Canadian people a chance to catch their breath. Before I sit down I should like to leave one thought with those engaged in industry. I do not purpose to speak for industry only; I happen to be a farmer as well, in common with many others in the house. But I do hope that industry will hear the echo from this sounding board of public opinion, namely, the Canadian House of Commons, and understand that we expect them to carry on and play their full part during this war-time emergency, even though they find themselves not able always to have a credit balance.

I should like to ask the minister with regard to what seems to me a vicious practice that has grown up; that is the practice of discharging men (who have been invalided home, and turning them over to the Department of Pensions and National Health for care and support. I do not remember a great deal about the last war; but if I remember correctly, my own father was in hospital for a considerable time after the war. In the last war if men were wounded or invalided home, they were a charge upon the Department of National Defence and received pay and allowances until they were discharged. I find now to my surprise several cases of the kind I have mentioned. Take one in particular, a young man wounded in England, and invalided home. I saw him during the Easter recess. He still has a tube in his side, and has a prospect of perhaps half a dozen operations. He now finds he is going to be invalided out, discharged from the army and turned over to the Department of Pensions and National Health. That department will be responsible for giving him hospital and medical care. I believe he can claim some $9 a week. If he were married it would be 813.50 a week. It may be necessary for this man to get treatment over a long time. It is not quite so bad for a single man, but
I had a case of a man who developed pneumonia, one lung being affected. He was discharged from the care of the Department of National Defence and put in a sanatorium as a civilian. His wife found her separation allowance stopped. When she came and told me about it I could not believe it, but I got in touch with the authorities and found it correct. He is now a civilian under the care of the Department of Pensions and National Health, despite the fact that he is not yet able to take his place in a civilian occupation.

I do not think my hon. friend objects to that; if he is discharged he would become a civilian. Then he is taken over by the Department of Pensions and National Health and given treatment. speechtext: The minister spoke yesterday of commando training and told us that a school was to be established in western Canada to give this new type of training. I suppose it would be difficult to expand that training to cover all the infantry recruits training in Canada, but would it not be a great help if that' commando training could be undertaken in Canada on a really large scale? Would it not help our army a great deal if several of these schools were set up and if eventually we could put all our infantrymen through such a school?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think I indicated yesterday that the purpose of the school was to train instructors, and the instructors are sent from the units. These instructors go back to the units; and I think I can say that the selection of instructors will be pretty general from all companies, and also from the trained soldier companies which are the graduates of the advanced training centres. They will be sending officers and non-commissioned officers as well to be trained. All my hon. friend is speaking of is the degree to which that training is to be done. We shall take into consideration what he has said about the comprehensiveness of it. But it is intended that the training shall get back to all the combatant units.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister mind making a statement at this time with regard to the situation at Debert camp? Complaints are coming through, from western men at least, as to the dampness and the difficulty of heating the huts. I have seen several complaints that men find it very difficult to acclimatize themselves to that area. I was wondering whether there has been an unusual amount of illness there due to camp conditions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Saskatchewan is making some reflections on the climate of Nova Scotia. I was at Debert camp last week, and the chief of the general staff was there a day or two afterwards, under conditions-I mean as regards rain-which I should think were about as unfavourable as they could be. I have taken up with the quartermaster-general certain matters with regard to the improvement of the camp and seeing to it that the roadways and the general means of communication are better. I did not hear a single complaint with regard to the heating of the huts. Of course it was then getting on to spring; it may be quite different in the winter time. I shall certainly take this matter up with the quartermaster-general.
As everybody knows, Debert camp was selected at a time when we were looking for a place which would give the proper operational location and be not far from the air force. It was ideal so far as the map location was concerned, because the air force had located a very large and useful aerodrome not far away. You cannot have everything. I believe that whatever natural disadvantages Debert camp may have by reasons of soil can be overcome; indeed they have been to a very large extent overcome in the year and a half it has been operating. I must pay tribute to the troops who went there a year ago last fall.
I know what it was like, for I was down there myself. It was, so to speak, in the forest primeval; conditions were not too good. Bat they went at it with a will, and I must say

War Appropriation
that some of the western units, particularly, gave one an extreme sense of satisfaction at the way they took it in their stride.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are good men, from the west.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I found one unit busying itself taking stumps out of the parade ground in front of their particular hut. But Debert camp has great possibilities, and I anticipate that we can overcome the difii-eulties my hon. friend has mentioned, although as a matter of fact I have not heard that the huts were cold or anything of that kind. Generally speaking, it is a fact that the soil is heavy, the water does not run off readily, and therefore drainage and roadways must have very much more attention paid to them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister has not
answered my other question: has there been an unusual number of cases of sickness at that camp?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I must say that I did
not ask about that. I was in the hospital- I believe, in every ward-and talked to the officer in command there. He did not mention that there had been any abnormality. The hospital was running well. I believe I asked a good many men as to their illnesses, and as far as I remember, hardly any of them mentioned colds or any affection which would arise as a consequence of damp weather. To answer my hon. friend's question directly, I have not heard that there was an abnormal amount of illness at Debert camp. I shall certainly make inquiries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We have been discussing for over two days questions connected with the army, and as yet we have had no statement from the minister regarding recruitment for the active army or for the reserve. The only statement which I have seen in connection with the reserve is that men are enlisting in large numbers. That statement did not come from the minister.
In so far as active service units are concerned I think we should be informed how many men have joined during the past two or three months, and whether the numbers joining are sufficient for the purposes of the army, not only to provide for its needs at the present time but also to meet the contingency of our men overseas being actively engaged.
During the last four or five days I have received a large number of letters from farmers and farmers' sons pointing out that, in spite of the announcement made by the Prime Minister on March 24 last, every consideration would be given to not calling up farmers' sons necessary in agriculture at this time, by granting them a postponement for the time being, the situation is veiy unsatisfactory. As far as those men are concerned who are actually in service, the promise was made that, upon application to the commanding officer, favourable consideration would be given to releasing men engaged in agriculture on leave to assist with the spring work.
In the latest issue of Canada at War, April, 1942, the following appears at page 8:
Emphasizing the vital role being played in this war by food, farmers, their sons and farm labourers are granted an indefinite postponement of compulsory military service if they are doing essential farm work. They may enlist as volunteers in the armed forces, but they cannot accept any non-agricultural work except seasonal employment. . . .
The situation in western Canada, especially in Saskatchewan, is no better than it was when the announcement was .made on March 24. I have had letters from men pointing out that they have brothers overseas and have been called up, although they are the only remaining young men on the farm able to cany on the operations. When applications are made to the national mobilization board, they contend that not sufficient attention is paid to them. I have every regard for the men who compose the national service board in that province, but I do not believe these applications are finding their way to the proper authorities. We are adjourning to-night for three or four days .-I wonder why an adjournment is being had at this time of grave seriousness-until next Tuesday. We who come from the far west find ourselves in the position of having come to Ottawa, to do the business of the country, to assist in doing it in any event, and yet an adjournment is to be made until next Tuesday. I mention that because if this matter is allowed to remain without some consideration being given to it immediately, the situation in so far as agriculture in western Canada is concerned will become most serious.
War Appropriation

I suggest to the minister that he should issue instructions to the various boards throughout Canada-this does not apply only to Saskatchewan-which would provide some common denominator of action for all the provinces. It cannot be that men are wanted in the reserve army. There is not such a rush because only the other day Major-General Browne issued a statement which appeared under date of April 20. I quote:
Things are rolling along with the Canadian reserve army, says Major-General B. W. Browne, director-general of that force.
^"They^took on 2,000 men in military district No. 2 (Toronto) last week and other districts are getting lots of recruits, too," he reported to-day.
If that statement be correct and if recruits are rolling into the reserve army; if men find their way into the reserve, why the necessity during the period between April 15 and May 15, to call up men who are on farms? They are willing to serve; all they ask is that the government carry out the promise which was made on March 24, not only in the House of Commons but in a radio address to the country. I suggest to the minister that if recruits for the reserve units are piling in, no harm would be done to this nation if these men were allowed to continue the necessary work of assisting in the spring work. Unless something is done at once, many parts of western Canada will not be placed under cultivation this year.
I am not asking for any different consideration for these men from that given to any other group. If they have not been called up yet, why the unnecessary rush since April 12? I ask the minister to give consideration at once to informing the national mobilization boards in the different provinces of the need of allowing as many men as possible to remain on their farms during the next three or four weeks, by postponements granted for that period, and that those who are in the service be permitted to return to their homes to assist in the spring farm work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned April 12, but I do not understand the significance of that date.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Two or three of the letters refer to being called up then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: From men?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Men on farms?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Men on farms who have been called up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I thought I understood the Prime Minister to make an announcement that men who were on farms, who were wholly or mainly engaged in the occupation of agriculture on March 23, would be allowed to stay on the farms.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is what was announced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have no doubt that the boards will deal with that. All a man has to do is to call attention to the fact that he is wholly or mainly engaged in the occupation. I do not know of any occupation in Canada-I think I am correct in saying this-the utility and usefulness of which in connection with the war activity has been so recognized as the farming industry. The army simply gives up any claim to those men who can show that on March 23, 1942, they were wholly or mainly engaged in agriculture. This is done regardless of how many there are on the farm, unless there are special circumstances. In other words, the burden is placed upon the army or the boards of showing that these men are not essential in industiy. I do not know what greater concession my hon. friend wants than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The promise is all right, and I am not complaining about the declaration of policy. I am simply asking the minister to have representations made so that the policy will be carried into effect. It is not being carried into effect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to know of a case where a man has shown the board that he was wholly or mainly engaged in agriculture on March 23 and has not been relieved, unless it was a case in which it was shown that he was not essential in industry. This comes under the Department of National War Services, but since I am representing the government here to-night I shall be only too happy to see that the matter is brought to the attention of the board. I thought we had that pretty well behind us so far as the army was concerned. We simply called it a day so far as the agricultural industry was concerned, except in those cases where we could show that a man was not essential in industry. In other words, the burden was on us. If he showed that he was wholly or mainly engaged in agriculture, I understood that the board would excuse him. If my hon. friend has some cases, I shall bring them to the attention of my colleague the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson).

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have found no difficulty whatever in having farmers exempted from military service. The only criticism I

War Appropriation
would make is that not enough time is given to the men in Regina who call up these men. In other words, you will want some men for April 12 and you send word out to Regina asking that they be called up. It takes rp to ten days for the notice to reach some of these men, and it will take four or five days or a week for the notice to get back. These men do not have sufficient time in which to ask for an exemption on the ground of being farmers' sons. I think more time should be given. In many of these places there is only one mail a week. There are some districts in my constituency like that. The mail may get there the day after it leaves the main centre, and then it stays eight or ten days before it gets out. Then it will take probably another week for it to come back. I ask the government to consider the advisability of giving these men a little more time so that they will have time to ask for an exemption. Otherwise, I think this is working out very well.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There would seem to be some mistake about the facts here. I called the adjutant-general to find out when the next two classes were called to report. I am not sure of the exact date, but it was between May 9 and May 15. I am sure it was no earlier than that, but I have an idea they had to report on May 15. By the way, the number for the first class is very small; I assure whoever mentioned one thousand men that there were not anything like one thousand men called in Saskatchewan in that first call. This is April 23; that is seven days until the end of the month; if the call is for May 9, that is sixteen days, and that call went out some time ago. That does not seem to me like too little time. I should like to get to the bottom of this thing, because on the facts as they are put to me there is ample time for these men to apply.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can assure the minister that what I have said is so. I went to Regina and saw the committee, and they assured me it was right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know what date he is speaking of?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have in mind that the next two calls are May 9 and May 15; both those calls have gone out now. But no matter what the facts are, I shall have inquiry made, because if there is anything understood by the Department of National Defence it
is that we have not much call on the agricultural community from now on as far as calling up men under the National Resources Mobilization Act is concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the policy of the various units with regard to granting requests for spring leave for farm work?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Just before I went west- that is three weeks ago-I received a communication from, I think, the president of the farmers' association of Saskatchewan representing that he thought it desirable that men have spring leave. I want hon. members to realize the situation. I am responsible for the maintenance and training, and operation if necessary, of the army in this country, and time is represented to us as flying fast. It is intimated in some quarters that we are not going fast enough.
I considered that my responsibility as Minister of National Defence would not permit me to give any wholesale direction with regard to releasing men who have come into the army, who have been trained or are in training, possibly for an operational role. The air force are not being asked to do it; the navy are not, and I did not feel that the army ought to be asked to undertake that obligation. At the same time I took occasion in Regina both going and coming to see the district officer commanding and discuss the matter with him. He fully realizes the situation and has taken up personally with Judge Embury cases which he thought or which Judge Embury might think were cases in which leave should be granted, and these are being considered. I went so rar, and so announced in the house, as to place in the hands of the board-which is separate from the Department of National Defence entirely, that is a board under the Department of National War Services, the power to say whether men should be relieved on compassionate grounds-that, of course, is the only ground on which these leaves could be granted-and we provided' in the regulations that the district officer commanding would take the recommendation or decision of the board in those cases notwithstanding the fact that the man was in the army: the only exception being one which you would expect, that is, if military exigencies were such as to make that impossible. That has been done and been discussed by me personally with Brigadier Trudeau in Saskatchewan, and I think, as far as can be, the serious cases are being attended to.
But I do feel that members of the committee ought not to expect me, as head of

War Appropriation
the Department of National Defence, endeavouring to mobilize, train and prepare an army for operation, to allow men in large numbers to go even for seeding operations. They are members of the army now; they had opportunity to apply for postponement; they did not, and I submit it is not fair at this time to ask that I simply issue a blanket order and say to the men, "Go home and do your seeding and then come back."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not ask that; I merely asked a statement of policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It would completely disorganize the training. We have men going through this four months' training plan; we have men going out in the first month, the second, the third and the fourth; we are not using the training facilities to the limit. I want hon. members to put themselves in my place and realize that I have some responsibility and that we cannot make a general declaration, much as one would like to. speechtext: Is that given by months?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

When the minister is bringing that information down, or perhaps at the

present time, could he tell the committee what forces in Canada make up what is called the reserve army, or the reserve force, in addition to these 44.S46 men? I believe there is a certain amount of confusion as to what makes up the reserve army.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend does
want me to give the list of the reserve units?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister whether I am correctly informed with regard to the extending of a military property at Barriefield. At the eastern side is a valuable property which produces large quantities of apples, and on which there is a good d-svelling; probably the west side is uncultivated land. I am informed just to-day that it is the intention of the department to expropriate the land to the east, and not the property to the west, which might be taken without putting any good, producing land out of production. As the latter property is vacant land, and the other property has produced in the last few years large crops of merchantable apples, I should be glad if the minister would look into the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If I had not looked into it already, I could quickly get rid of the question, by saying that I would do so. I can, however, assure my hon. friend that I have looked into it. I had a senior officer of the department with me for over two hours, looking over the map; I have had the real estate people and the engineers down there;
I went to the trouble of telephoning the real estate adviser who was in Toronto; I have talked to Mr. Harvey, who owns the land; and we have come to the conclusion that this property is necessary to the development of the training centre which we are building. We realize it looks peculiar to be taking an apple orchard for use as a training centre; but we have examined the cost of developing any other site to which we have been referred, and we find that, apple orchard and all, the cost will be considerably less than if w'e took another property. Further, the property just to the west is rough ground which cannot be used so advantageously. It would make a very poor location, indeed for a camp. The ground across the road is the ordnance training centre, which will be extended, and our only way of extension is toward the east. The development we propose has already grown three times greater than was originally planned, and we expect that it will grow even more. I have not myself looked at the ground, but I have examined its location on

War Appropriation
the map and have seen the people who have to do with it in the department. I am advised that there is not a chance of making a reasonable job of extending the camp, providing the necessary room for expansion, and at the same time providing a training ground, without taking that property.
Another property there, known as the Cartwright property, has been offered to us more than once. Though I am not crying down that property at all, it, too, is rough ground; my hon. friend probably knows it much better than I d-o. It does -not seem to be suitable for camp ground. We estimated that the cost of putting in the services and building a camp there would be greater than the additional cost involved in the purchase of the property my hon. friend has in mind, putting a camp there, and having room for development in the future. For better or worse I have passed the -project. I have advised Mr. Harvey, and I think he understands the situation. I believe he would have preferred to keep the farm because he has just bought it, but what we regard as the paramount interests of the service made it necessary that we should take it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Could the minister -give the committee a break-down of the figure of 44,846 men who were called up und-er the National Resources Mobilization Act; that is, how many of these have gone into the active forces, how many are now on home defence, how many have gone into the reserve army, and how many, after finishing their period of training, have returned to civil life?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have that information -here. The important thing which my hon. friend wants is, I think, the -percentage of active enlistments, and I am sorry I do not have it -for all the services. I can tell him that the percentage of active enlistments of those called up to report from March 20, 1941, to October 2, 1941, was 36 per cent. That is, 36 per cent of those accepted enlisted in the active army, the air force or the navy. I have not a -break-down of percentages as between the three services; but, roughly speaking, the division is 25 -per cent -for the army, 10 per cent for the air force, one per cent for the navy; that is, of active enlistments.
My hon. friend asked me how -many had returned to civil life. Of course he realizes that, of those who have -been- called- up, none have been returned to civil life unless they were discharged on account of being medically unfit or something of that kind, because they were all called up for service. -If my hon. friend wants the information, by tracing through the record of each individual I could
tell him to which units they have gone after they have come from the training schools, -but I d-o not believe -he would ask me to do that.
The chief of the general staff reminds me that my -hon. friend also asked how many went into the reserve army. None of these would go into the reserve army; all would be called up and be on full-time service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister gave a statement of enlistments from January on in the active army; would he also give us the number discharged during the same period?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have not that here.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
During the last two days there has been some discussion about the reserve army, and perhaps this house might be of considerable assistance to the reserve army at this time. They have fallen upon better days at long last. As the minister explained yesterday, about three weeks ago a director-general of the reserve army was appointed in the person of Major-General Browne. I think General Browne gave the picture quite clearly when he was quoted as saying at that time:
"The reserve force may have to fight and it must be ready to fight as soon as possible," be said.
"After all, there is no more war overseas than there is here now, and we may have some here sooner than they have, in view of the threats to our coast."
In other words, as I see it, the reserve army has now been given its proper role, the defence of Canada in the event of an attempted invasion. General Browne has also been quoted as saying that he hoped the reserve army would be recruited to a strength of at least 150,000 men. Yesterday the minister told us, as reported on page 1861 of Hansard, that as of April 9 the strength was 71,737 men in reserve units, 5,062 men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act and 1,523 men employed on training centre staffs. This gives a total of a little over 80,000 men.
There has been some talk to-night about the men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act; but as I understand it, apart from the 5,000 odd, they have become part of the active force although they are only for service in Canada. The men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act do not become part of the reserve army as it was described by the minister last night.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The only National Resources Mobilization Act men who are part of the reserve force are about 60,000 men, the 30-day men who have not been recalled.
War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The 60,000 men to whom the minister now refers are men who took the 30-day course last year and who have now gone back to civilian life. They are merely names on the walls of the different armouries across Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It depends on the unit, really.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Generally speaking, I think my statement is correct. The 80,000 men who now compose our reserve army are largely men who have enlisted for the defence of Canada. They are not in the younger age groups, being mostly over 35 years of age. There has been some complaint that men are not rushing to enlist in this reserve army, and it is in that connection that I think the house could be of great help. When I was in Vancouver during the Easter recess I found that many men had the impression that if they joined the reserve army, they might be sent off to guard a railway somewhere and kept there for months. That made it impossible for them to enlist. They were perfectly willing to serve in an emergency; they were prepared to train and fight if the country were invaded, but they simply could not give up their businesses and their families and go away to do guard duty. In other words, the feeling was that they should be used for an emergency. I believe that it is the intention of the Department of National Defence that these men should be trained and will be used only if there is an emergency of that type. I feel perfectly confident that if the minister will announce that to be the case; if he will say that this reserve army is to defend the homes of Canada in the event of an invasion; that that is the purpose for which he is calling for recruits for the reserve army, he will be surprised at the response he will receive. Members of the house could help a great deal by spreading this news throughout their ridings. In that way we could help a great deal in the recruiting of this reserve army.
Conditions in Vancouver with regard: to the reserve army have improved greatly within the last few days. For example, the night I left home there was a parade of the reserve brigade. I believe that this was extremely impressive and that many men made application to join after the parade. Another thing that was done was to have all the officers and men in the reserve units wear their uniforms to work, whether that was delivering milk, in a store or in an office. The idea was to impress the general public with the fact that the reserve force was really worth while and that there were excellent citizens serving in 
that force. I think the result will be to increase enlistments. Therefore I suggest to the minister that he make a statement to-night to the effect that the reserve army is to defend the homes of Canada; that that is the purpose for which it is being raised.
I have another suggestion to make. I think consideration should be given to changing the present rule with regard to the enlistment of married men. Until a day or two before we left here in March the reserve army was not allowed to recruit married men under thirty-five years of age. Then the minister announced a change and said that men from thirty to thirty-five years could be recruited in the reserve army. There are many younger married men who cannot join the reserve force at the present time and yet who are not subject to call under the National Resources Mobilization Act. As the committee knows, that act applies as yet only to single men and widowers without children up to the age of thirty years. Married, men may not be called for a matter of months or perhaps even a longer period.
I realize that the idea in not allowing them to enlist in the reserve army was that this might push them into the active force by the back-door. The hope was that, not being able to join the reserve army and not wishing to be still in civilian clothes, they would join the active force. I think the time has gone by when methods of that type should be used. These young married men should be allowed to go into the reserve force at this time. Physically they are the best group we could get into the reserve force. They are entitled to have training to be able to defend their homes and families just as much as the men over thirty years of age. Even though they are eventually to be taken into the active force under the National Resources Mobilization Act, or go in voluntarily, they should be given the chance to get training in the meantime. It would be of great advantage to them, and I believe that under the regulations as they stand at the present time they could still be called up for service in the active force even though they had enlisted in the reserve force. If I am wrong, perhaps the minister will correct me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is the position at the
present time. There could be no question that they were sheltering from the active force by joining the reserve force.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They would not be
"sheltered", to use my friend's word, from being called up, but they would be sheltered in this way, that they would be in the reserve

TFar Appropriation
army and perhaps would not feel the same urge to join the active army. I am interrupting my hon. friend, but let me say that this rule with regard to age limit did not come from the Department of National Defence; it was made on a suggestion to me personally by officers of the reserve army, who felt that the reserve army was being used, in some cases that they knew about, as a place where men went and felt that they were doing their full duty. It was the view of those officers that the reserve army was not intended for that purpose and that it was not quite fair to them in the reserve army to have that situation existing. I do not think it was some invention by someone who wanted to see that everyone was forced into the active force.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have had suggestions to the opposite effect made to me by officers of reserve units. Perhaps the viewpoint is changing a little as time goes on. There is a need to fill up these reserve units without further delay. I throw out the suggestion that the minister consider the position again, and if he does not wish to allow all married men in, he should at least allow men in, say from twenty-five to thirty years of age.
Another suggestion is that consideration be given to appealing to men in war industries to join these reserve units. For example, on the Pacific coast the role of the reserve brigade is of vital importance in the event of attack. It seems to me that the men who are working in war industries might be very badly needed in the reserve brigade should an emergency arise. I suggest that an appeal be made even to men in war industries to give up two nights a week and perhaps some time at the week-end in order that they may get at least some military training.
Then I think the department cannot be too careful to see that these reserve brigades are given at least enough equipment of all types with which to do some training. There has been that difficulty that men have joined these reserve units, found that there was no equipment and then became disgusted and left. There is a new enthusiasm now growing up, and I think this is the time to see to it that they get some at least of every type of the equipment with which they would be equipped were they fighting. They are all very keen; they have all had considerable experience in civilian life, and they are particularly interested in the new types of equipment and the more advanced training. I suggest that the department treat them with that condition in mind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I appreciate the spirit in which my hon. friend approaches this matter and the interest he has taken. I think every
point he has made has been made at these meetings of reserve officers which I have attended. The suggestion he makes with regard to some declaration respecting a limited role for the reserve army-I put it in that way-was made to me in Vancouver. It has not been made to me anywhere else. I do not say that by way of reflection at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think the reserve is more badly needed there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Three very responsible
officers came to see me about the matter and left me a memorandum, and it has troubled me considerably. But I say frankly that I am a little cautious about undertaking any obligations with regard to methods of using troops, particularly in view of the situation which faces us in this country to-day and the fact that we are having a plebiscite on a statement of that kind made some time ago. I want to be just as fair as I can and to encourage enlistment in the reserve army; but I do not want someone coming to me and saying, "You gave us a pledge or an assurance that we would not be used elsewhere than in our home community, and now you are taking us somewhere else." I heard my hon. friend say, "except in an emergency" which, of course, is an elastic phrase. But I have not shut the door on the idea. The reserve army has a place in the Militia Act, and everyone knows what the duties are. People should join the reserve army with the realization of the full implications of that duty, whatever they may be. I feel that they can join the reserve army with some confidence that they will not be called on unduly, but for me to say under just what conditions they will be used and under what conditions they will not be used, is something I hesitate to do.
A statement was prepared which I was asked if I would sign. It was prepared in a most careful way. The gentleman sought to make it as easy as possible for me to make that statement. It did not tie one down very much, but it was to give the impression at least that the reserve army would not be used outside the particular community or area in which it was mobilized.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
May I interrupt to point
out that I carefully avoided saying that they should not be used in other than their own communities. I said, to defend the homes of Canada; if the Atlantic or the Pacific coast were attacked, it would be understood that men from Ontario or Quebec would go, and I am sure they would do so gladly, to fight on either coast. But I mean, for example,



War Appropriation
that they should not be taken and put on full-time guard duty or be sent outside Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have my hon. friend's representations. They are along the lines of representations I have received and they are being considered. The committee will understand my reluctance when I say that there is a specific place for the reserve army, and whether one should say anything indicating a limitation of its duties is something which should receive a good deal of consideration. Of course there is less consideration required when my hon. friend suggests that taking in men twenty-five to thirty-five-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Married men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
One of the arguments
which might be put forward for indicating a possible modification of the duties of the reserve army would be that the men were between thirty-five and fifty; but when you say, "no, we are going to put in men twenty-five to thirty-five and give them assurance that they are not going on coast defence duty or guard duty," that makes it more difficult. The suggestion was made at Halifax as to the age limit, and I told the officers there frankly that I could not agree to that alteration in the age limit.
My hon. friend mentioned another point with which I am particularly concerned; that is, men in war industries. I thoroughly agree, I think he has the right point of view, the point of view I tried to express yesterday. A man has the satisfaction of working at a lathe in a war industry, he feels he is doing a good job for the country, but his conscience is bothering him a bit as to whether or not he should be in uniform. The reserve army gives him an opportunity to work at his lathe and to turn out in uniform and be ready to do other duty if necessary. It seems to me that has an attraction for many of our citizens who want to do their duty; it gives them two chances instead of one.
I feel also that the appeal should not be only to war industry workers, but in some cases to employers, not only in war industry but in others as well. I have found a case or two, one in particular, in which I remember a man writing to me reporting that a man had refused to give him employment if he went into the reserve army. That came up at a conference, and I have taken it up directly with the firm concerned.
I do want to say generally that when my hon. friend speaks about war industries and workers in those industries, I feel that we should and I believe we can enlist the interest of the employers, who will not discourage but

will rather encourage their men, though they are doing good work where they are in connection with the production of munitions, to give at least two or three of their evenings to do this very important part of our war activity. I propose to do that at a very early date, and I appreciate the suggestion of my hon. friend that members of the House of Commons should do the same thing. I would ask them sincerely to join in influencing the people around them to do this. There is nothing formal about this work in connection with the reserve army. It is a real job; it is going to take some time, and perhaps occasionally it is going to be grim. I often think that people would far rather do without some ration of gasoline, do without tires and pay more taxes, but that time and particularly comfort are two things we find it hard to sacrifice. The reserve army does cut into comfort; there is no doubt about that. It does not leave men free in the evenings; they cannot play bridge or go out to entertainments, or anything like that, after a hard day's work. But this is something we have to do if we are going to win this war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about equipment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I can only say to the
committee that I have dealt with that matter at every place we have gone. General Browne and the master-general of the ordnance have gone over the equipment situation thoroughly with the chief of the general staff. As I indicated yesterday, some priority will be given in connection with equipment. I can only say that the last bit of equipment that is available for the reserve army will be given to them; but that must always have regard to the necessities on the active fronts, as everyone understands. Someone said to me in Saint John, "You do not need to worry about equipment. You tell us that you will give us all that is available, and we will not expect anything more." Of course they cannot expect anything more, but we will try to make available everything possible, having regard to the needs of the active forces. Production certainly is increasing; there are some particular items in which the reserve army will, I think, be better served than ever before. I am sure we are not making any false moves in connection with this matter. We are asking the reserve army to improvise to some extent, as it always has done; to put up with one piece of equipment where it would like to have two or three. I believe we can make a success of this movement, which will make a splendid second line in connection with the defence of this country, should the worst come.

TPar Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
A few moments ago the minister said he would bring down a return in connection with the reserve army. When he does so, would he be good enough to break down that return as between infantry, rifle, machine gun, tank, artillery and so on?
I was pleased to hear the minister say a moment ago that at last the reserve army had a real job to do, and would be recognized to a greater extent. The minister mentioned the eleven brigades that have been set up for the reserve army. Those, however, will accommodate only about one-third of the reserve force units. I fear that- perhaps the minister is forgetting those other, orphan battalions and units which will not be included in these brigades. They are located in small cities and towns; in fact, some battalions are decentralized and split up between perhaps three, four or five different places. I think the minister will admit that in the days gone by, the reserve army supplied a great many instructors and men to the active force. At the present time one of the great difficulties in the reserve army is that they sadly lack qualified officers and noncommissioned officers for instructional purposes. The minister said yesterday that about a thousand officers and men had returned from England to act as instructors in Canada. I would ask if at least some of those instructors could not be allotted to various reserve force units.
Another point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is that when a reserve force unit covers perhaps one or two communities, very often there is a distance of from fifty to a hundred miles between battalion headquarters and some of the company headquarters, and in attempting to carry on training there is that age-old difficulty of who is to pay the travelling expenses of the officers, non-commissioned officers and men who come to company headquarters to carry on drill at night, or to take part in week-end manoeuvres. I am sure this question has been a headache to the department in days past, but it is most important to the men, who are paid only a matter of some sixty cents for one night's drill. If they have to use their own cars and gasoline and oil in order to come to headquarters for training, I believe some plan should be worked out under which these men might be reimbursed in some way for their travelling expenses. I should like also to point out to the minister that now the question of gasoline is going to be of vital importance. Many of these men have to travel fifteen or twenty miles in order to
44561-121i
take their training, and I believe they should receive some consideration in connection with their gasoline allowance.
I was pleased to hear the minister state that every possible consideration will be given to the reserve force units in the allotment of equipment. I am sure the minister will agree when I say that nothing discourages the average recruit so much as to carry on continually with parade ground drill and lectures, with perhaps only an old Lewis gun for training. Naturally these young men are greatly interested in the newer forms of automatic weapons; and if the minister could give two or three or four of these newer weapons to each reserve force unit, I am sure that in itself would create a great deal of interest and assist materially in the recruiting of new men. Perhaps the minister might be able to tell the committee in some detail just what equipment he hopes to be able to furnish to the reserve force units. The minister shakes his head. He will realize, I am sure, that at present the average member of a reserve force unit has a rifle and a bayonet, and that is about all, with perhaps one or two old Lewis guns for the whole unit. If they could be assured that they would be given some of these newer weapons, or if they could be told in some detail what they may hope to get, it would be of great help in bringing in new men.

speechtext:
While we are in this
part of the discussion, would the minister feel it advantageous to the committee to make some observations by way of explanation relative to the allocation of various men in the army? There are many cases which might be taken into consideration, and concerning which the public might be enlightened. For instance, about a month ago we had a report to the effect that 150 senior officers overseas, in England, were being replaced by younger men. Those officers were giving up their rank, and coming back to Canada. Could we have an explanation as to what use has been made of those officers in Canada? We have the case where officers, non-commissioned officers and lower rank are being brought from England to take special courses in connection with officers' training corps instruction in Canada. What particular use is the government going to make of those men? Are they going to be retained- in Canada for instructional purposes? Are they going to rejoin their units overseas, or are they going to form new units in Canada?
What is the position of the department with regard to draftees who volunteer for active service? Does the army try to place them in the particular branch for which they are best adapted?
Then, take the veterans of the last war, too mature in age and perhaps not physically strong enough to stand the strain of overseas service; what particular use is the department making of them?
There is also the Canadian Women's Army Corps, which has been formed to take over certain duties in the armed forces.
There are a great many places in the army where these classes of people can serve their country efficiently and release those who are physically fit for more active service. Guard duty, mess duty, driving of cars and trucks, patrol duty, clerical work, and perhaps the less exacting kind of administrative work, are all branches of service in which various classes of people can be usefully employed in the service of their country, and I think the
War Appropriation

public would be pleased to have the assurance from the minister that the government is giving consideration to the proper allocation of those who are offering their services by way of draft or otherwise, taking into account their capacity, aptitudes and physical condition, and the duties they may be called upon to perform.
Fatigue duty has been discussed, and it was pointed out that the training of a soldier is not complete until he has had considerable training in fatigue duties. That is true, although it can be carried to excess, but undoubtedly certain forms of service do not call for as exacting qualifications as other forms.
Another question that comes to my mind, which I have been asked several times, is this: What assurance is given to the ladies at present in the Canadian Women's Army Corps, [DOT]that, while possessing other aptitudes, they are pot to be taken away from the particular spheres of endeavour for which they are qualified and in which they wish to serve?
I think it would be of great interest to the country if the minister would make a detailed statement along the lines of my suggestions and assure the Canadian people that the government is giving serious consideration to this matter, just as it is giving consideration in the mustering of the army to certain age groups, the restraining of employers in certain industries from giving employment to men of military age, and matters of that sort.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What my hon. friend has last referred to is probably one of the most interesting and important phases of the whole army programme, or of any war programme. It means trying to put the right man in the right place and trying, if one possibly can, to save a man who is best equipped for a' certain job to do that particular job, letting somebody else perform a less difficult one. We have tackled that question in the department in a realistic way. There has been no fanfare of trumpets about it, but we have a personnel selection board under the adjutant-general, headed by Brigadier Chisholm, who has personnel selection officers at all the basic training centres, officers' training centres and district depots. Do not let me mislead the oommittee. That branch has been functioning for not more than six months, but already we have seen a marked usefulness and an improvement through its efforts. Everybody, of course, cannot do that work. We have had to some extent the benefit of personnel people from industry who have come in and helped us. We have tried to keep the idea of psychology out of it. I think it always scares a man to be put through a psychological or

I.Q. test. What has been done has been by way of interview and by wTay of test at the same time. The soldier will talk to a man who understands judging men, their mental capacity and mental aptitudes. Such a man will talk to a soldier for, it may be, only ten minutes, give him a test and be able to estimate pretty accurately his general capacity, and then endeavour to steer him along the line where that capacity can best be used. If statistics mean anything, at the present moment the number being tested and interviewed in Canada is 22,000. We have not a big staff; and when the committee realizes that we have 60 training centres across Canada, it will be understood that it takes a big staff to cover them all. But we have these staffs operating in every basic training centre, in the officers' training centres and in the depots.
To give the committee an idea of the results of these tests, 61 per cent of those taking them have been given normal placement in the armed forces; that is to say, they were found fit for the job they enlisted for. Thirty-four per cent were recommended as trades trainees, having particular aptitudes, regard being had to their previous training or to their whole mental outlook; for 3-7 per cent there were special recommendations, such as for special appointments or transfer to other services. If a man who has enlisted in the army is particularly adapted to the air force, I do not think the personnel selection board are averse to seeing the man go where he will give the most useful service. Then 1-2 per cent have been set over for further examination. Altogether there have been examined, interviewed, to be dealt with further, no decision or final classification having yet been made, 76,000 men. Therefore that particular branch of the service has been working at top speed.
That is what is done, and that is apart from what is being done every day in any well-regulated institution, and in every organization. The senior officer is over these men, and the non-commissioned officers are keeping an eye on them to see where they can best be used. When you have an army which contains, in some branches, 35 per cent of tradesmen you have to keep a watch upon them all the time. We are doing that; it is being done by the officers as well as the men. But this personnel selection branch is a growing concern, and we have got great value out of it.
As regards the use of C category men-I refer to that because it is generally illustrative of the class to which my hon. friend refers- he understands, of course, the battle which is going on and has been going on since the beginning of the war, and is now, I believe,

War Appropriation
intensified: that is to say, we are not using an A man for a C man's job. That applies particularly to the depots. I suppose that if the adjutant-general has one headache more than another, it is with relation to the depots. When men get into the depots it is difficult to get them documented, inoculated, and passed on to the next stage, to go to the training centre, because they are pulled off for this duty and that. The depot seems to be the place where you can get a man for a job, it may be a fatigue or what-not. We try to see that the administrative part of a depot settlement is filled as far as possible by low category men, so that active men can be spared for the service for which they were intended and for which they enlisted.
With regard to over-age officers, nothing *would give my hon. friend the information to which he refers except a nominal roll of each officer showing what disposal was made of him. I have in mind the list which came over about January 1, when the age limits were put into effect. I believe that very few of them have retired-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: About one hundred and fifty.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
-and I understand that many of them were absorbed in England at holding units, training centres and places of that sort; they were simply taken from field formations. As the committee knows, a number have returned and taken positions here, and they are, of course, proving exceedingly useful, because they have experience of the training and operations which are taking place in England. I believe that, generally speaking, they are giving an extremely good account of themselves.
With regard to the junior officers who are coming back, not as instructors but to take the junior war staff course, they will be utilized both in England and in Canada. I would not want General McNaughton to hear me say this, because I believe he has in mind that most of them will go back to the staff in England. But the search for capable young staff officers will never cease, and the men who are coming back here are needed to do real jobs when the crisis comes.
With respect to the instructors, I mentioned yesterday that about a thousand officers and non-commissioned officers have come home. They will probably stay here about eight months at their work, and they will then go back to England Some of them, we hope, can be spared to join units here and help strengthen the forces in Canada wherever they may be most needed. Certainly it is a great stiffening of our training to have them come
over here. At the same time it gives them a change and an opportunity to utilize their experience of the training they have had by imparting it to others.
This is very general and, I am afraid, sketchy. But the big point which my hon. friend made, and the one to which I want to refer, is, first, that we are trying to make use of the best in the men in order to get the greatest utility possible out of their capacity; and, second, we are trying to save the more active men to do the more active jobs.
The chief of the general staff reminds me in reference to the cadres we are forming now for the seventh and eighth divisions- for that matter, for the sixth division also- that for every cadre of officers and noncommissioned officers we form here for these units, a certain number are brought back from England. It is some recognition of their services there and it helps us here. As an illustration of that, just before I came in the house to-night I approved the recommendation of the selection board of no less than ten officers who are now overseas to commands in Canada. All of them have been recommended by our staffs over there to take commands here. If I published a list of these it would be quite a striking thing. I do not believe that the public of Canada understand how many men who have served in England are in this country at the present time and bow much help we are getting from them, nor do they realize how many are going to England. I find myself losing count of them; a week goes by and when I ask for this or that man I find that he is in England with an n.c.o. or two, attached to some battalion over there in order to get experience. This constant interchange is going on.
In reference to the Canadian Women's Army Corps, I speak subject to correction, but I do not believe that the personnel selection board have actually taken on work in relation to that corps. Primarily they are devoting their attention to four branches: one, dietetics, which includes cooking and waiting as well; secondly, clerical; thirdly, auxiliary services; fourthly, motor mechanics and things of that sort. The corps is, I think, making a great success. We are very much pleased with the work which has been done in the training of them at the school at Macdonald college. Accessions to the ranks have not been as rapid as we should have liked, not because of any lack of applications but because it is so difficult, with all the building that is going on, to provide accommodation. The committee will understand that we have had some difficulty in providing accommodation in camps, training centres and
War Appropriation

places like that for these young women, but it is being overcome, and overcome very rapidly. All the reports I have had about the work which these women are doing indicate that they are quite capable of taking the places of the men in the jobs to which they are assigned, and there is no doubt that they will be the means of saving a very substantial amount of man-power. I am extremely pleased and proud of the way in which they have carried on.
