subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is not only the problem of making an intelligent allocation of men in the different branches of a service; there is also the problem of allocating men to the different services themselves. I know this is a ticklish and delicate problem, but sometimes fools rush in where angels fear to tread. Has any thought been given to this? I know of men who have trained in the reserve units and would have made first-class soldiers or non-commissioned officers. They went, however, into the air force as members of the ground crew. There is a certain glamour about that force; they have natty uniforms, and it seems to be attractive to the young men. I know a number of these fellows. They are splendid physical specimens, all in category Al, and yet they are members of the ground crew.
Has there been any collaboration between the army and the air force with a view to meeting this situation? I do not know enough about the matter to speak categorically, but from a layman's point of view it would seem that men in B category could do the work of a ground crew. I cannot understand why a man who is short-sighted or who has flat feet could not service a plane in an aerodrome. But that has not been done. As I say, many of these men in Al category are members of the ground crew in the air force. The day may come very quickly, should another front be opened up and there be many casualties, when we shall need as many Al category men in the army as it is possible to get. I know the Minister of National Defence for Air will not appreciate my suggesting this, but this problem will have to be faced. Probably

War Appropriation
it should have been faced earlier in the war.
Is any attempt being made as between the different services to allocate men? I know it is a difficult thing to say to a man that he should not join the air force, that he should go into the army or some other service. On the other hand, if one service has a waiting list as they have in the air force, and the army is just making its quota month by month, sometimes as a result of terrific work by the recruiting officers, something should be done. There has been a definite tendency for men to go into the one service. It is too bad when the government has spent a lot of money and the army a lot of time in training men, that they should go into a different service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am afraid I can give my hon. friend only a very brief statement. Naturally, what he has said is not open to argument. There has been, not only consultation but collaboration with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air. There is this to be said with regard to the ground crew. From the very beginning of the air training plan it was recognized-I was going to say 50 per cent-that a very large percentage of the activity of the air force would be in the ground crew. I shall not give the figures to-night, but most hon. members know the small number of air crew there is compared with the ground crew in a squadron. The real mechanization of Canada's army came later, and many of these men were already in the ground crew.
I do not argue for one minute against what my hon. friend has said about the possibility of our being able to utilize these men in the lower categories in connection with the air force. I would not want to be taken as saying that this is the case because I do not know enough about the air force and its service requirements. It may be that only certain men can stand up to the needs of the service. This matter has been the subject of earnest, thoughtful and intensive discussion between myself and my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air. We have an interdepartmental personnel committee which is considering how best we can help each other in connection with the matter of recruitment. We try not to step on each other's toes, but to assist one another. The matter of joint recruiting offices was considered, but there were reasons which I need not go into to-night which seemed to make that impracticable. We have always had the arrangement that one would send a man to the other if he seemed more fitted for a particular job.
I do not think I can say anything more to my hon. friend. I shall take note of what he
has said and bring it to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air. This is discussed, I may say, at defence council more often than my hon. friend may believe. We are all endeavouring out of a limited field to get the men we need for the different services. So far, we have been able to do it. By this personnel selection board we think we are improving that situation, and we hope that it will result in the very best allocation of men possible, having regard to their capabilities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the army responsible for the defence of air fields and airports, or is that the task of the air force? That is a very important question, particularly in northern British Columbia and the Yukon, and on both coasts. There has been considerable trouble and difficulty about it in Great Britain. Has Canada got around that difficulty?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The army accepts responsibility for the defence of air fields. I regard it as the army's job to see, if possible, that the enemy is kept far enough away that the planes at the aerodrome can get into the air. We do that by anti-aircraft guns and by keeping paratroops from landing on the field and things of that sort. Once the planes are up, they take care of the situation themselves. But it is the defence of a post, just as the defence of a naval base.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is recognized as a job for the army?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I know of no intention to make any change in that respect. We have some construction battalions in England.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In yesterday's Montreal Star there was a dispatch from Victoria stating:
British Columbia may give Canada and possibly the United States, a new defence arm -the motor boat and automobile "emergency transportation squadrons". . . .
Harold Husband, representative of the Dominion Department of Transport here, disclosed that squadrons were being organized on Vancouver island and the "blueprints" would

War Appropriation

be made available to other parts of British Columbia and Canada as soon as possible. They also may be sent to authorities in the United States if there is any interest in them there.
Then, it goes on to describe the work of these transportation squadrons, which apparently is to supply automobiles and also motorboats for emergency transportation. Does the Department of National Defence know anything about this move?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have not heard anything yet. My hon. friend has the credit of having brought it first to my attention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will send the clipping to
the minister and perhaps he might investigate. I think there is a good deal of merit in the suggestion.
Another question is with regard to what used to be known in the last war as the paper war. We get complaints repeatedly, relating to all three services, that there is far too much correspondence, too much passing the buck, letters from this department to that department and so on right down the line. Two or three months ago I had an unsigned, anonymous letter from an officer in the force; strictly speaking I suppose I am not entitled to read it, but he had some very good suggestions. I should like to read the one dealing with correspondence:
Speed-up of interdepartmental correspondence. At present the red tape that ties up interdepartmental business is dreadful. Officers and men are often kept kicking their heels about for weeks at a time doing nothing while their papers (documents to us) are undergoing some mysterious process. 1 myself had time to take five weeks training in another branch of the service while my papers were undergoing this process, and when they did call me in the papers were confused and nobody seemed to know where I was to go, so I went back to sitting in the mess reading the morning papers and enjoying life for another ten days, at $5 a day. Surely a telegraph service could be installed in each camp for the use of routine business, it would be an excellent training ground for the signal corps. In one case a letter from Ottawa was sent west for an officer to be dispatched east to catch a draft, the letter was mailed with a three-cent stamp. The time lost was made up by the officer being brought east by air travel. A good telegraph service linking every camp in Canada would be excellent training for the signal corps and put our Canada army in Canada on a war basis.
I realize the difficulty. In all our business, civilian as well as military, there is far too much letter-writing, but probably the army is very prone to develop in that direction. I's any attempt being made to cut out some of this letter-writing and, if so, what?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I could show my hon. friend cases that make that one pale into insignificance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Doesn't it make you mad1?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No one knows better than the army the difficulties that exist. Constantly, steadily, all the time, slowly but persistently I think we are improving in that respect. Some most radical things have been done at headquarters with regard to cutting red tape; the trouble is, the organization is so big and has grown so fast, there have been so many people appointed who have to have a look at a thing and consider it, that it takes a long time to get around1. If a man could go to one man's desk and have him stop his work and attend to that particular thing you would get that through splendidly, but you would not get the day's work done. You must have some system. I have in mind now an improvement which has taken six weeks to get through, but I am sure it will result in a great deal of labour saving.
The difficulty in connection with army administration is to separate the big from the small. That is, each thing has to take the same amount of time, no matter how important or unimportant. The trouble is, a return may be asked for in the house in connection with something that amounts to only $100 which may cause more back-fire than something amounting to $10,000. That is why everyone is concerned in seeing that things are done regularly. But we have to take some chances in connection with the army as with everything else, and verbal instructions are given sometimes and confirmed afterwards on the file.
At the last district officers' meeting, instructions were given about this point of postage, that the telephone could1 be used and used freely in order to hasten matters, because a letter has to go to some central distributing office and so on. With thousands of letters in a day, it is the next day before the letter gets to the department; it may be the next afternoon before it gets to the officer who has to attend to it, and he may have to send it to different places to get notes in regard to costs and materials and so on. We are short-cutting to a reasonable extent, I think; we are toiling slowly upward-I would not say through the night

but we are making definite progress in that respect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the situation any better in Great Britain? Have they any better system? If they have, we might copy it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not want to comment. I am willing to say that anyone's

War Appropriation
system is better-I do not believe it, but I would not want to say that anyone's system is worse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Certainly not in stenographic help.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No. But, you see, we
have had officers who have been at the war office. The former chief of the general staff was there for three or four years, and we have had other officers attached there. I believe we have adopted anything from there that has seemed useful.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What about this suggestion
that there should be a telegraph service between the camps? Is that feasible, or is it not? If a telegraph service could not be instituted, what about a wireless service? Would that not be possible?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is at present a
complete wireless service between districts. I think what my hon. friend means by a telegraph service is the up-to-date apparatus called the teletype. We have spent a good deal of the money of the people of Canada in connection with teletype service, and it has been of tremendous help. I do not want to make a public statement as to where the teletypes are located, but they are working every minute, and we are having to increase the number. We know they are well worth it, not only in connection with the money saved but in the efficiency produced and the speed with which we can get on.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They come under the signal corps, do they?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. In some instances
one service puts them in and then puts in switch lines to the other two services. In other words, they just have the one teletype set for out-of-town service, and the three branches get the benefit of it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister has made
a very fair but extremely limited statement on the allocation of men. Perhaps he cannot enlarge upon it, but I am not yet satisfied that a useful purpose would not be served if we could be told a little more about the way a man seeking to enter the army is put in the place for which he is most fitted. I have in mind several cases which have come to my attention, perhaps more by hearsay than by direct contact. It seems to me that when a man goes to join the air force he is given almost every consideration in being directed to that particular branch of the air force for which his trade, training or experience best fits him. On the other hand, it seems to me that in the army, if you do not go to a particular unit, there is no place where you can get information as to the branch of the ser-44561-122.}
vice you should enter. With most of the recruiting depots being depots for all units, veiy little guidance is given to the recruit seeking to enlist, as to the particular unit or particular branch of the service he should enter.
One case drawn to my attention a short time ago was that of a man with experience in electrical engineering. Then, not two weeks ago another case was brought to my notice, that of a man who had perhaps five years' practical experience in connection with precision tools. In common with many other people he did not feel like sacrificing that experience by going into the ranks in any particular branch of the army, without some assurance that full use would be made of his training. I wondered whether the minister had given consideration to the position of the average man, who does not know as much about military life as he might, who has some special qualifications and who does not know where he can secure guidance as to the possibility of his particular knowledge being used in some particular branch of the service. Perhaps the minister might explain that a little more fully.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should be very much
surprised if one statement made by my hon. friend should be true. He said the recruiting offices were recruiting for particular units. That is not intended. If the recruiting officer is doing his job-and I have seen a good many of them; I have met them at conferences, and I have an idea they are on the job-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not mean to cast
any aspersions on any recruiting officer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I appreciate that; but I believe these officers are qualified to do exactly what my hon. friend asks about. That is to say, my hon. friend is quite right in suggesting that a man is entitled to all the advice and all the information he can get about the particular branch of the service he would like to enter. But what I wish to impress upon the committee is this, though it may sound a little impersonal. First of all, a man has to make the decision as between the army, the navy and the air force. If he decides to go into the army; if he will only enlist for general service, I will undertake that when he meets these personnel selection people he will find them sympathetic; he will find that they know what the army has to offer, that they know.what qualifications are required for a particular branch. They will find out from him what qualifications he possesses, and they will put him in the right place. A man may say, "I want to be a signaller." He has a right to say that; that is his own decision.
War Appropriation

But if he wants help, I really think he should enlist for general service and then take the advice of these personnel selection people as to where he should go if he really wants full use made of his abilities. That is pretty simple, but I really think it is sound.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I can appreciate that viewpoint in one who is, as it were, looking from the inside out, but according to the minister's explanation it puts a man with special qualifications in the position that, first of all, he must join for general service. He may have some diffidence about trusting his future to general service without first knowing-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He does anyway.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is so, but not with the same degree of recklessness, perhaps, as he does when he joins for general service. Consider the man I mentioned a moment ago, with five years of technical experience. Apparently he had taken special training and had considerable experience in connection with precision instruments. He wanted to join some branch of the army in which he would have some reasonable assurance that he would use that experience, and would have an opportunity further to develop himself as well. From the inside looking out, one might be inclined to say that he should join the army for general service and trust to the efficiency of the army, about which he knows nothing, to put him in his proper place, to see that he gets proper pay and proper promotions. Yet it would put him much more at ease if, before signing on the dotted line and joining the army, he could be given much more guidance than, in my uninformed opinion, he gets now. I believe this point might be well worth consideration, and perhaps the minister might give a little further explanation in that regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have suggested the
method. We try to have the recruiting officers well acquainted with the needs of the various arms of the service. They try to size up a man, and I am really satisfied that most recruiting officers would be willing to give any man helpful, sound and useful advice. If it would help, I would set up a bureau anywhere, but that is what the recruiting officers are for. We have also formed these civilian committees to assist in that direction, because often a man does not want help about a technical matter but rather information about what his duties will be. It seems to me these civilian committees can be of great assistance in this regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not want to suggest that this situation does exist; but very often a man, not knowing the army, not knowing the officers, has every reason to feel that

he possesses qualifications which should entitle him to a higher rank than that of a raw recruit just entering the army. Though perhaps I should not say so, frequently people are led to believe that, to some extent at least, you need a little pull, a little assistance or a little drag to get the better positions in the army. That very situation leads to that opinion, in so far as it may prevail.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have said all I can
about the matter of drag. I know that is the feeling not only about the army, but about almost everything-it may be the church, or anything else. It seems to be the idea that if you want to get anywhere, you must get someone to speak a few words for you. But I believe that the army is about as clear of it as it has ever been, or as any organization is.
Any man with the qualifications of a machinist, or with other technical qualifications, will be snapped up so fast, and will be taken so quickly, that it will certainly make his heart warm, if he is enthusiastic about the service. It is not a question of drag; it is a matter of taking advice, and of being satisfied with and having confidence in the person who gives it. We will do our level best to see that a man will not think he is being influenced by people inside. If he does get into the army, we will shift him around so that he can go to the place where he serves best. Having done that, I believe we have tried to serve him as best we can.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any definite rule of procedure a boy in the service should follow? He may know that he possesses mechanical skill and may wish to be transferred to some other unit where that skill might be useful. Under such circumstances, what procedure would he follow? I have been told it is contrary to the rules for him to write to his member of parliament, and it seems there is no one else to whom he can write. If he happens to be shy, he does not wish to be paraded before his superior officer, and may not have the ability to express himself. Under those circumstances he might remain a long time without recognition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not a matter of
recognition. My hon. friend has put his finger on something which I know always presents some difficulty, and that is that the young man in the army feels that he cannot apply to his commanding officer. I am preaching and always have preached-and I believe I am sound in this-that an officer as nearly as possible ought to be a father to his men. By that I mean that that young fellow should immediately apply to his platoon officer-

War Appropriation
and he does not need to be paraded, either. The platoon officer will talk to him at any time. He might go to his commanding officer and ask to be transferred. If his qualifications are mechanical, he will be readily picked up. There is a general comb-out-I believe that is^ the right word to use-of all units. Men with mechanical qualifications are taken quickly. Without my hon. friend using any pull, or anything like that, I should like to know of any case in which that would not work. I do say that the young man should first of all exhaust that way of doing things. I say that because it is just this procedure of writing to a member of parliament, and something happening as a result of it, that gives the impression there is some sort of drag.
I believe that if the young fellows would go to their officers,' if those officers are the kind of men they ought to be they will see that ability is recognized. This pressure is not coming from below only; it is coming from the people above, as well, who are looking for these men and who are trying to get them to go to the trade schools at Hamilton, Barrie-field, Woodstock and other places where trades are being taught.
Just the other day a father came to me and, naturally, wanted me to write somebody on behalf of his son. I said, "I cannot do it; but tell your boy to go to his platoon officer." I have not heard from him since, and I do not know whether he took my advice or not.
That is another thing about soldiering; I do not think they teach the boys enough about army procedure. I should be very much surprised if the procedure I have suggested would not work, if the boy had the qualifications I assume he has.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My experience has been that the minister's officers are very considerate, once a matter like this is brought to their attention. They do manifest the interest the minister would like to have them show. But at the same time several cases have been brought to my attention where the boys were just too shy, and they did not know what to do. When I was approached I did not know what to tell them to do. The minister says they should approach their sergeant-major?
Mr. RALSTON; Their platoon officer. Those boys probably have not a platoon officer; they probably have instructors. Probably the boy whom the hon. member has in mind is in a training centre, and is not in a platoon. If he is in a training centre, he will surely be caught, because the comb-out officers will be all around the training centres looking for men with mechanical ability. If he is in
a unit, have him go to his platoon officer, or speak to the officer commanding. He does not necessarily have to parade before the commanding officer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The training centres are organized in platoons, are they not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. But with all due respect I never think the platoon officer in a training centre is quite as close to his men- because he knows his men for only a short time-as the officer who is in a unit and expects to have his platoon permanently.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I know what the minister has suggested is being done very often. I know some of the platoon commanders in some training centres, and I know that is what they are doing. A few weeks ago I had dinner with a young platoon officer, and he showed me that he was keeping a record of each man who went through his hands, to show what his aptitude was. I think a great deal more of that should be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: At six o'clock I believe we were talking about that, and I am delighted to hear it is being done. I have felt that in this war the army is too impersonal, the fault being possibly that of the training centres. We are trying more and more to impress upon the officers that their biggest job apart from training the men is to look after them and be a sort of father to them. When an officer sees that a man is in difficulty he should help him out, even though that man does not happen to be his man for all time. The officer on the job has charge of that man, and is responsible for his comfort as well as for his work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any delay with regard to promotions in the forces now in England? I have in mind a chap from the west who is in England, and who is an experienced druggist. He has been over there for more than a year. Although I have not done anything about the matter, it has seemed to me that there has been some difficulty with regard to getting his promotion confirmed on this siue. Are the officers in charge on the other side permitted to make promotions over there, or do they have to be recommended from Ottawa?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They may make promotions over there, up to a certain rank. I am sure that rank is probably far above the rank to which my hon. friend's friend expects to be promoted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is that rank?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I can say that it is up to lieutenant-colonel; I shall not say anything

further than that. I do not imagine my hon. friend's friend will plan going any higher than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He is still a private.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then I can say he need not await approval from this side.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If a boy's parents desire that he go home to work on the farm or to put in the crop, whom should be approach? The rule is that he must approach his commanding officer, is it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I have known several boys who have been at a loss to know whom to approach. They felt somewhat shy about the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They should approach their commanding officer, through the platoon officer or whoever happens to be the officer next to him.
Progress reported.
